v3.23.0

Section titled “v3.23.0”

Published 2026-10-19 · Updated 2026-10-19 · View on GitHub

What’s new

Section titled “What’s new”

Features

Section titled “Features”

The workflow guard is now opt-in: installations without an explicit workflow_guard.mode use disabled instead of observe. To keep the previous behavior, set {"workflow_guard":{"mode":"observe"}} in your user-level systematic.json. Explicit observe and protected settings continue to work as before. (#1158)

A disabled guard now skips operation observers, repository snapshots, session-history reads, and receipt classification, removing the 19 startup git calls it previously made even when explicitly disabled. Its four workflow tools remain registered, and completion calls return a terminal disabled rejection instead of staying pending.

Guard guidance is now included only in OpenCode sessions where the guard is enabled. Pi and Claude Code no longer receive instructions for a guard they do not run, reducing their bootstrap by about 2.4 KB. Configuration schemas and documentation reflect the new default.

Also in this release

Section titled “Also in this release”
  • deps: Updated fro-bot/agent to v0.123.1. (#1150)

Compare

Section titled “Compare”

v3.22.7…v3.23.0

v3.22.7

Section titled “v3.22.7”

Published 2026-10-18 · Updated 2026-10-18 · View on GitHub

What’s new

Section titled “What’s new”

Bug Fixes

Section titled “Bug Fixes”

The workflow observer now reads file contents inside submodules and untracked nested repositories, rather than checking only a submodule’s path and HEAD. Edits, untracked files, and nested changes now affect the snapshot digest and prevent commit closure, while a dirty submodule leaves the snapshot available. Unborn submodules are also readable; uninitialized submodules no longer prevent commit receipts after a plain clone or in a new linked worktree. See #1151.

File, gitlink, and byte limits are shared across the parent and every walked repository. Changes to a walked repository’s root, Git directories, or HEAD during a snapshot are detected as an unstable worktree. The digest domain advances to worktree:v4, so completing a unit that was in progress across the upgrade may require retrying after a stale-receipt rejection.

  • release: Updated release metadata for v3.22.7.

v3.22.6…v3.22.7

v3.22.6

Section titled “v3.22.6”

Published 2026-10-18 · Updated 2026-10-18 · View on GitHub

What’s new

Section titled “What’s new”

Bug Fixes

Section titled “Bug Fixes”

The workflow guard now rejects observations superseded by a changed unit declaration, unit completion, or mode change while classification is in flight. A declaration-generation fence prevents evidence from being accepted under a declaration it was never checked against. Seed timeouts also remain visible when a baseline was propagated from pull-request creation: the affected operation retains its before-read retry, while admission still checks against the propagated baseline. (#1144)

Workflow-guard test fixtures now isolate their Git commands from inherited routing variables and global or system configuration, and supply fixture identities per command. This prevents those fixtures from writing identities or commits into a caller’s repository when Git environment settings leak into the test process. The change covers this fixture runner; isolation of other test helpers remains a separate follow-up. (#1148)

Documentation

Section titled “Documentation”

The solution guides now explain the declaration-generation fence and the propagated-baseline seed-timeout rule, including their limits. Architecture and plan notes were corrected to match the implemented behavior, including removal of a seed-replacement scenario that the guard already prevents. (#1146)

Also in this release

Section titled “Also in this release”
  • Updated Fro Bot Agent to v0.123.0. (#1149)
  • Updated Playwright to v1.64.1. (#1141)
  • Release version bookkeeping for v3.22.6.

Section titled “Compare”

v3.22.5…v3.22.6

v3.22.5

Section titled “v3.22.5”

Published 2026-10-17 · Updated 2026-10-17 · View on GitHub

What’s new

Section titled “What’s new”

Bug Fixes

Section titled “Bug Fixes”

The workflow guard can now recover when the worktree prevents a snapshot: it blocks the affected unit instead of disabling enforcement for the session. Completion reports the block reason, and stale receipts or worktree changes during completion can be retried after the underlying problem is resolved. (#1134)

Transient operation timeouts and rejected pushes are also confined to the affected call rather than making the guard permanently unavailable. A skipped or sealed call may already have run, so check local or remote state before retrying. Verification runs that overlap another local call no longer earn a receipt—even if the tree is restored before verification finishes. Rerun verification alone after all local calls return. (#1138, #1142)

Security fixes update remaining nested js-yaml v4 copies in docs and release tooling to 4.3.2, addressing YAML denial-of-service vulnerabilities. The release GitHub client’s undici dependency moves to 7.30.1 to preserve custom connection/TLS checks and address that consumer’s cache-disclosure and WebSocket denial-of-service advisories. (#1137, #1139)

Documentation

Section titled “Documentation”

New solution records explain recoverable snapshot blocks, the async-commit version fence, defensive checks that cannot be proven, call-scoped timeout and push failures, and why overlapping verification is sealed. They preserve the reasoning behind these guard behaviors for future fixes. (#1136, #1140, #1143)

Also in this release

Section titled “Also in this release”
  • dev: Update TypeBox to 1.3.37. (#1133)
  • release: Version bookkeeping for v3.22.5.

Compare

Section titled “Compare”

v3.22.4…v3.22.5

v3.22.4

Section titled “v3.22.4”

Published 2026-10-15 · Updated 2026-10-15 · View on GitHub

What’s new

Section titled “What’s new”

Bug Fixes

Section titled “Bug Fixes”

The local operation observer now checks worktree content independently of Git’s clean filters and configuration, preventing changed files from appearing unchanged and stale evidence from being reused. Snapshots include HEAD paths dropped from the index and ignore-rule contents, compare raw file bytes and modes against HEAD, and refuse snapshots when repository anchors move or content changes during the read. Submodule checks distinguish uninitialized and displaced paths, while length-prefixed digest fields prevent ambiguous tree identities. These changes close false-clean paths that could otherwise allow an uncommitted edit to mint a commit receipt. (#1129)

PostCSS’s compatible Nano ID dependency is resolved to 3.3.20 to address the denial-of-service advisory GHSA-2v37-7h3g-55p8, with manifests and other locked packages unchanged. (#1127)

Documentation

Section titled “Documentation”

New solution records capture the digest-collapse, release-gate, brokered-push and action-pin fixes, along with the operation observer’s false-clean fixes and the review-spiral scope cut, preserving those findings for future work. (#1122, #1130)

Tests

Section titled “Tests”

Release tests no longer tie the App token action to one specific commit, avoiding test failures on Renovate updates. The step test checks the action’s identity, while the shared action-pin test continues to require a full 40-character commit SHA and a version comment. (#1121)

Also in this release

Section titled “Also in this release”
  • deps: Update actions/create-github-app-token to v3.3.0 (#1102), fro-bot/agent to v0.122.2 (#1123), and github/codeql-action to v4.39.0 (#1132).

v3.22.3

Section titled “v3.22.3”

Published 2026-10-14 · Updated 2026-10-14 · View on GitHub

What’s new

Section titled “What’s new”

Bug Fixes

Section titled “Bug Fixes”

Guarded workflows now fingerprint full-length identities and operation arguments. Previously, identities longer than 1,024 characters shared a constant digest, hiding changes, while write, edit, and patch arguments longer than 8,192 characters could make an active guard unavailable. Identity hashing now includes the complete trimmed value, and argument serialization removes the size budget while retaining its depth limit. JSON-encoded state fields preserve field boundaries, and validation rejects non-plain objects and symbol-keyed properties before patch canonicalization can hide them. (#1119)

Sessions without active guarded work no longer pay for before-and-after worktree snapshots. Operations are observed only while an epoch is active or an allowlisted skill load is pending; skipped operations also stay silent when after-hooks arrive more than once. This avoids unnecessary snapshot overhead and prevents unrelated snapshot failures from disabling the guard. (#1116)

The scheduled release gate now accepts GitHub-verified release commits whose committer is web-flow, matching commits created through the GitHub API. Every commit must still be authored by the release App, and an App committer remains accepted. This fixes the gate refusing release PRs produced by the refresh job. (#1120)

Security fixes bound indexed source-map processing, patch the Sharp librsvg vulnerability, and reject injected URI authority components. (#1060, #1059, #1052)

Continuous Integration

Section titled “Continuous Integration”

Trusted comments on same-repository PRs now anchor checkout and brokered push to the resolved PR head SHA, so fixes are delivered rather than losing the agent’s local commit. Fork heads remain refused. The brokered push also permits changes to skills, agents, tests, and registry files while keeping workflow files, scripts, manifests, and lockfiles denied. (#1117)

The hourly release reconcile has been removed: pushes to main already refresh the release PR, and publication follows the merge of an approved release PR. Recovery remains available by rerunning or dispatching the Release workflow while main still points at the release merge. (#1112)

Miscellaneous Chores

Section titled “Miscellaneous Chores”

The Biome schema now matches the installed release, and Renovate updates the schema alongside the package. This release also records the v3.22.3 release commit. (#1056, a3e4273)

  • deps: Update fro-bot/agent to v0.122.1. (#1114)

Published 2026-10-13 · Updated 2026-10-13 · View on GitHub

What’s new

Section titled “What’s new”

Bug Fixes

Section titled “Bug Fixes”

Loading a skill no longer starts an unrelated guarded workflow. Previously, unrecognized skills were treated as ce:work, so loading ce:review, ce:brainstorm, or another skill could demand implementation evidence, reopen a completed unit, or collide with an active shipping workflow. Only ce:work, git-commit, and git-commit-push-pr now activate a workflow epoch, with or without the systematic: prefix; other skill loads leave guard state unchanged. (#1107)

Bundled workflow handoff targets now resolve, and skill instructions and review persona descriptions use loadable names such as ce:plan, ce:brainstorm, and document-review instead of directory-form names that caused not-found errors. Content-integrity checks reject stale names in code spans and prose while preserving paths, filenames, qualified agent IDs, and fenced code. (#1110, #1111)

Tests

Section titled “Tests”

Real-host guard tests now verify that skill loads actually succeed, rather than accepting the absence of guard markers as sufficient evidence. The non-allowlisted ce:plan scenario confirms output exceeding 32 KB and an inactive guard on a follow-up status call; the allowlisted ce:work scenario also checks the size threshold. Coverage additionally pins the fail-closed outcome when a skill name changes between hooks. (#1109, #1107)

What’s new

Section titled “What’s new”

Bug Fixes

Section titled “Bug Fixes”

The workflow guard can now snapshot larger repositories without becoming unavailable on the first shell command: local limits rise to 128 MiB of file content, 20,000 files, and 8 MiB of listing output. Remote readbacks retain separate limits of 4,096 items and 1 MiB, so larger local snapshots do not loosen remote bounds. (#1101)

When a hook makes the guard unavailable, status now records a bounded, enum-only cause and the hook site instead of a bare unavailable state. Initialization failures are recorded, protected mode rejects tool calls when no guard can be published, and history confirmation preserves an already-recorded hook failure. Diagnostic causes exclude raw exception messages, including potentially sensitive file names. (#1101)

Continuous Integration

Section titled “Continuous Integration”

Releases now publish only by merging the gated release pull request, with npm authentication through OIDC trusted publishing. The legacy publish path and RELEASE_MODE switch are removed. Release follow-on workflows rely on a GitHub release authored by the release App as evidence that npm publishing completed, avoiding failures caused by registry visibility delays. The real-host contract check is required on main, and recovery documentation covers both a failed npm upload that leaves a tag and an npm publish whose GitHub release is missing. Release narration also uses the runner’s permitted scratch directory. (#1100)

The release pull-request refresh job now runs even when the upstream publish job is skipped, while still requiring a successful render on main. This fixes ordinary merges rendering a release pull request without opening it. (#1103)

What’s new

Section titled “What’s new”

Features

Section titled “Features”

Releases gain an approval-gated path: a release-app pull request carries the pending version and its CHANGELOG.md entry, previewed with semantic-release’s existing version rules. In gated mode, publishing requires approval on the exact pull-request head from the maintainer or an attested scheduled gate. The approved changelog entry becomes the release notes, and a version mismatch stops publishing before a tag is created. (#1094)

The scheduled gate checks the release pull request against current main and all required checks before approving it. A release hold blocks gate-only publishing and is read live immediately before publication. Reconciliation refreshes the pending release, preserves approvals when its contents are unchanged, and handles superseded or already-published releases. RELEASING.md documents the cutover, holds, verification, and recovery procedures; a generated docs changelog shows entries through the deployed release tag.

Continuous Integration

Section titled “Continuous Integration”

Release-note rewriting runs in its own workflow, and documentation builds use the published release tag so the deployed docs correspond to that release. (#1092)

The release pipeline separates read-only preview and build jobs from credentialed publishing. Claude Code plugin publication moves to a dedicated post-release workflow that waits for the version to appear on npm. Repository rules require an approved pull request for changes to main and restrict release branches to the release app; Fro Bot approval is limited to maintainer-authored pull requests without Fro Bot commits. (#1094)

Workflow-guard readback timeouts no longer disable the guard for the rest of the session after an operation has succeeded. What’s new

Section titled “What’s new”

Bug Fixes

Section titled “Bug Fixes”

The workflow guard now defers only the affected remote operation when its activation probe times out, rather than permanently disabling the entire session. The unit and epoch stay active, and the deferred operation remains required. Its own before-read can establish a baseline from the same observer and target, with one retry on timeout. A push with no upstream also defers instead of disabling the session, though that first push still cannot produce a receipt.

PR creation now establishes its baseline from the after-read only when the before-read reported a missing resource. Timed-out or failed before-reads no longer admit a PR-creation receipt as though no PR had existed. Check and review readbacks retain their deferrals when their before-read reports a missing resource. Other activation-seeding failures remain fatal. See #1082.

What’s new

Bug Fixes

Section titled “Bug Fixes”

The workflow guard now reports a session that has not started a guarded workflow as inactive / no-active-epoch, reserving unavailable for genuine failures. This prevents agents checking status first from treating an idle session as terminal and skipping completion enforcement. Status calls no longer poison fresh-session initialization or discard pending sibling operations, and completion before a workflow starts returns a guard-owned rejection rather than an error. Unavailable status also exposes a bounded diagnostic cause, while failed history reads continue to fail closed. See #1079.

Section titled “Documentation”

The architecture guide now explains the optional arguments parameter on systematic_skill: supplied arguments replace $ARGUMENTS and positional $N placeholders, or are appended when the skill has no placeholders. This documents how callers pass task-specific input into loaded skills. See #1078.

v3.20.0…v3.21.0

v3.20.0

Section titled “v3.20.0”

Published 2026-09-20 · Updated 2026-09-20 · View on GitHub

What’s new

Section titled “What’s new”

Features

Section titled “Features”

A repository can now ship the model routing it depends on. Until this release, a repository that declared its own OpenCode provider had no way to distribute the routing that consumes it. Project config could select a named profile but never define one, so the routing had to live in every teammate’s global config — unshareable by cloning, and dead weight in every other repository. This release adds allow_project_profiles: when a user turns it on, a repository’s project config may define its own profiles map (#1011, 7fbecd0).

The guarantee is that a project-defined bundle supplies routing only where user-owned config is silent. It can never override, and never partially clobber, a value you set. That holds structurally rather than by policy: the overlay chain is normally user base → active profile → project → custom, but when the active bundle came from project config it is placed first instead, so user base merges over it. Nothing checks “is this allowed” — the ordering is the guarantee. Merging is field-additive one level into the opencode and pi blocks, reusing the same mergeProfileOverlayValue a normal profile already uses, with only the argument order differing, so next wins each field it sets and the other side fills the gaps.

Whole-entry replacement was the alternative, and it fails concretely: setting opencode.variant on an agent whose project bundle sets opencode.model erases the model, leaving a qualifier with no model — which assertRoutingInvariants rejects, breaking the whole config load because you customised one field. There is a test for exactly that case. Because the guarantee comes from two separated code sites rather than a single check, a test pins each one; the ordering test was verified to fail for the right reason, reporting the project’s losing value where the user’s should be. ARCHITECTURE.md states plainly that the guarantee is a consequence of the implementation as written and is not separately enforced.

The opt-in is itself protected. allow_project_profiles joins workflow_guard in a new PROJECT_ALWAYS_PROTECTED_FIELDS set stripped from a project source unconditionally, and its effective value resolves from custom and user config only — a repository cannot grant itself the permission. A project config that sets the opt-in and ships a profiles map in the same file gets both stripped, which is covered by a test. profiles moved out of the always-protected set into a conditional strip, the only behavioural change when the opt-in is off; with it off, everything is byte-identical to before, and the existing test locking project-profile stripping passes unmodified. Name collisions cannot shadow either: bundle lookup is custom, then user, then project last, so a user-defined name always wins, and SYSTEMATIC_PROFILE still overrides which profile a repository selects for itself. SECURITY_OVERLAY_FIELDS is untouched and ProfileOverlaySchema remains routing-only, so a bundle is structurally incapable of carrying permission or skills — which is what keeps this a narrow surface.

Two supporting changes ship alongside. Config sources previously loaded user → project → custom, but the opt-in can be set in OPENCODE_CONFIG_DIR config, which outranks user, so a custom-set opt-in was unknown when the project source was parsed and stripped. User and custom now load ahead of project, with the alias machinery — where project and custom can resolve to the same file — re-verified against its existing tests unchanged. Separately, because advisory semantics make “the bundle applied nothing” a normal outcome, a bundle fully absorbed by user config would otherwise be indistinguishable from no bundle at all. config show now reports Defined in: naming the file that defined the active bundle, and each routing field carries an origin (user, custom, user-profile, custom-profile, project-profile) alongside the existing shape provenance, so full absorption reads as every field user-origin while a project profile is active. Origin is tracked per merge step rather than derived from the overlay entry’s sourcePath, which is last-writer-wins and would misattribute a field whose value survived from an earlier step. Both surface in --json as activeProfileSourcePath and per-field source.*.origin.

Section titled “v3.18.8”

Published 2026-09-18 · Updated 2026-09-18 · View on GitHub

What’s new

Section titled “What’s new”

Bug Fixes

Section titled “Bug Fixes”

ce:review now carries the route narrowing reason all the way to finalize and the artifact. This closes the last gap left open by #984, where the behavior was pinned by a test rather than fixed.

deriveRoute requires a route_narrowing_reason whenever the model proposes a route narrower than the meet over a finding’s contributing survivors. That rule worked at merge time and was inert everywhere after it. MergedFindingSchema carried the resulting route — autofix_class, owner, requires_verification — but not the reason, so the finalize-phase verifier reconstructed a proposed_route from those carried fields and fabricated route_narrowing_reason: 'carried route verification' to get past the guard. A check that constructs its own passing input cannot fail.

The consequence was downstream and silent: partitionFindings routes strictly on owner, with no severity carve-out. A finding whose owner narrowed to release left the fixer queue for report_only — so a P0 could drop out of actionable work with nothing in the artifact recording why.

The reason now travels on the merge wire and onto the persisted finding, and finalize checks it against the real meet in both directions: a route narrower than the meet must carry a reason, and a route equal to the meet must not — a reason without a narrowing claims a decision that was never made. The second half was missing entirely, not merely unenforced. This adds a new reject reason, merged finding route narrowing reason mismatch.

The pairing is enforced in the pipeline rather than in the artifact schema, because the schema cannot see contributing survivors and therefore cannot compute the meet. That constraint is documented inline where a reader would otherwise expect a superRefine, alongside the existing validated/validation_reason rule it resembles.

Contract impact: review-summary-schema.json gains one optional field. schema_version stays 1 — the field is additive, so existing artifacts still validate. findings-schema.json and review-pipeline-schema.json are byte-identical: reviewers do not author route narrowing, and the reviewer-facing shapes (ParentFindingSchema, SubAgentFindingSchema, SubAgentReturnSchema) are untouched.

Verification: the behavior-changing assertions were confirmed failing against unpatched sources before the fix, so they test the gap rather than the implementation. Coverage includes a narrowed route with no reason, an unnarrowed route carrying one, a narrowed route whose reason reaches the artifact, and the specific P0 → release → report_only path that motivated the change. tests/unit/review-pipeline-finalize.test.ts previously pinned the permissive behavior; it is updated rather than removed and now asserts the reason is carried. 3106 unit tests pass, with typecheck, Biome, content-integrity, and all four drift gates clean. (#998, 9d45da3)

v3.18.7

Section titled “v3.18.7”

Published 2026-09-18 · Updated 2026-09-18 · View on GitHub

What’s new

Section titled “What’s new”

This patch closes the diagnostic half of systematic config show — a broken config now explains itself, and reports failure the way a script expects.

Bug Fixes

Section titled “Bug Fixes”

config show now tells you why a config failed to load. The prose renderer printed Resolved configuration: unavailable (the configuration failed to load). and stopped — no file, no key, no reason — because a bare catch in printResolvedSection discarded the Error object. The --json renderer never had that gap: buildConfigShowJson bound the error and returned its message, so identical input produced a useful explanation in one rendering and a dead end in the other. Nothing in the code or docs suggested the prose form was meant to be less informative; the two catches were simply written differently. The failure report now carries a Reason: line with the same message --json returns, naming the offending file and key (#995, 555595a).

This deliberately does not relax the rejection itself. A project-level agents.*.model or categories.*.model overlay is still refused by design as a trust boundary; the change only ensures that if the failure is meant to be hard, it at least says why.

The same failure now produces a non-zero exit and lands on stderr. After the diagnostic fix, the two renderings agreed on the reason and disagreed on everything else: config show exited 0 on a broken config while config show --json exited 1, and the earlier test had pinned that 0 rather than flagging it. A script or agent invoking the default form read success from a config that had not loaded. printResolvedSection now reports whether the load succeeded and configShow exits 1 when it did not. The report also moves from stdout to stderr in full, so config show 2>err.log no longer yields an empty error log beside a non-zero exit — splitting a two-line report across streams would leave either half unreadable on its own. The --json envelope stays on stdout on purpose: that document is the machine-readable output, error field included, and consumers still pipe it to jq (#997, 3019c96).

Both changes were verified across rejected, valid, and absent project configs to confirm the healthy paths still exit 0. The regression tests pin the two renderings to each other — matching exit codes and matching reason strings against the same broken config — so a future divergence fails regardless of which side moves. Exit codes are now stated in the model-profiles guide, which previously described what config show prints but not what it returns.

Bug Fixes

fix(deps) (#991, 7707bb3) rolls the non-major dependency group forward on two fronts.

zod moved from 4.6.4 to 4.6.5. Zod is the runtime schema layer Systematic’s config parsing depends on, so patch-level movement here touches every config-validation path. Upstream, 4.6.5 keys the .properties() shape off the instance type for z.instanceof() schemas (colinhacks/zod#6600) and settles the z.currencyCode() churn from the prior patch — it was reverted and then restored over a vendored ISO 4217 list refreshed weekly by CI (colinhacks/zod#6595). The rest of the upstream delta is documentation folded into the 4.6 release post.

The shared workflow dependency bfra-me/.github moved from v4.29.0 to v4.30.0. That bump is itself a rollup: bfra-me/renovate-action advanced across 10.39.0 through 10.42.1, fro-bot/agent advanced from 0.112.0 to 0.113.2 inside the reusable workflows, and pnpm moved from 11.26.0 to 11.27.0. What’s new

Section titled “What’s new”

A documentation-focused patch. The substance of this release is a new docs/solutions/ entry capturing a defect class that survived three independent rounds of review, plus routine dependency maintenance.

Documentation

Section titled “Documentation”

docs(solutions) adds re-verify-carried-state-at-phase-boundaries-2026-09-15.md, a learning drawn from building the ce:review synthesis pipeline. The same defect appeared five separate times in one place: the seam where a phase hands derived state to a later phase that must re-verify it rather than trust it. Three separate passes of scrutiny — a read-only architectural review, running the pipeline against its own code, and two rounds of PR review — each found instances the others missed, and every blocking finding from the final round landed in a seam the earlier passes had already inspected.

The recurring shapes were a wire projection that dropped derived fields and forced the consumer to re-infer them; a verifier fed the very field it was testing, so a tampered value plus a matching dependent value round-tripped cleanly; joins that checked presence but not completeness, so a deleted request passed as satisfied; a “by construction” argument living inside a verifier whose entire premise is untrusted input; and two derivations over different row sets whose reconciling invariant was documented but never asserted.

The reason this matters beyond ce:review: every bad envelope was schema-valid. Strict Zod contracts and a clean typecheck caught none of them, because shape was never the problem. One case needed no adversarial input at all — any run with an unavailable reviewer emitted an artifact whose counts disagreed with its own ledger. The document states seven checkable rules with before/after excerpts from the shipped implementation, names the concrete consequence class (forged dedup identity, laundered confidence, misattributed ownership, and artifacts that do not reconcile with themselves), and describes the recognizable situations where it applies.

It was written through ce:compound in full mode. Overlap against the nearest prior art — the artifact-contract learning from #793 — scored Moderate, so this landed as a new document that cross-links to it rather than an edit to the existing one.

Published 2026-09-15 · Updated 2026-09-15 · View on GitHub

What’s new

Section titled “What’s new”

The ce:review synthesis pipeline is now executable code instead of prose instructions the model had to follow by hand. That is the substantive change in this release; the rest is dependency repinning.

Bug Fixes

Section titled “Bug Fixes”

ce:review previously asked the model to perform deterministic synthesis manually — confidence gating, candidate grouping, provenance, route narrowing, action queues, counts, sorting, and risk coverage were all prose instructions. That produced non-conforming artifacts on the first try, drifted between harnesses, and left “the same evidence yields the same report” as an aspiration rather than a property. #984 moves synthesis into code, closing #795.

Four pure phases now live in src/lib/review-pipeline.ts behind a strict Zod contract (src/lib/review-pipeline-contract.ts) and ship in the bundled helper skills/ce-review/scripts/validate-review.mjs, which every harness already resolves through SKILL_DIR:

  • screen admits one raw reviewer return, binds it to the dispatched persona, and extracts rejected severities as bounded enum values. Admission depends only on the payload, the expected reviewer, and the harness — the shell environment cannot change it.
  • prepare applies the confidence gate, groups admitted findings into candidate pairs by normalized file, and unions selection surfaces.
  • merge validates the model’s adjudication as a strict partition over the prepared candidates, then derives each merged finding’s severity, agreement-boosted confidence, fingerprint, submitters, and conservatively narrowed route, returning the exact set of findings that need a validator.
  • finalize re-verifies every cross-phase join, re-runs the merge derivation over carried survivors as a verifier, reconciles validator outcomes, derives dispositions, counts, action queues, and replacement risk coverage, routes plan-assessment results, and emits either the schema-parsed review-summary.json artifact or a report-only projection. Both modes pass the same integrity gates.

The model keeps what only it can do: adjudicating candidate groups, judging validator evidence, assessing the plan, and rendering the report. Stages 4–6 of skills/ce-review/SKILL.md now call the phases at their decision boundaries, with invocation blocks and envelope shapes documented in the new references/pipeline-invocation.md, explicit never-bypass rules for helper failure, and an atomic temp-file write for the artifact.

Carried envelopes are treated as trust inputs, not proof. finalize rejects a tampered severity, confidence, file, or route; a duplicated or missing dispatch record; a survivor cited twice; a citation of an unavailable reviewer; a forged validation state; or a screen result that disagrees with its dispatch record. Diagnostics name the failing phase and, on a pipeline rejection, the fixed reason and safe path — never payload content.

Existing artifact consumers are unaffected: review-summary-schema.json and findings-schema.json are byte-identical at schema version 1, and only review-pipeline-schema.json — covering the model-authored envelopes — is new. Verification covered 3,038 unit tests including roughly 330 new ones across the contract and each phase, a packaging test that runs all four phases under real Node from the npm, OCX, and Claude Code layouts, and an integration test that drives a complete Stage 4–6 run plus an equivalent report-only run through a real OpenCode host.

What’s new

Section titled “What’s new”

Features

Section titled “Features”

ce:review now validates each raw persona return before parsing, screening, or persistence. The new bounded, stdin-only validator rejects empty, oversized, invalid UTF-8, malformed JSON, and schema-invalid payloads without writing them to disk, while keeping diagnostics payload-safe. Review selection is also risk-based: correctness, testing, and project standards form the core team, and maintainability, agent-native, learnings, deployment, and other specialists are selected only when the changed repository surface warrants them. Selection reasons remain visible in coverage, and failures from risk-critical reviewers stay blocking rather than disappearing from the reported team.

Documentation

Section titled “Documentation”

The architecture and structure guides now document review-artifact cleanup’s preview/execute safety model, the paired .context ignore prerequisite before persistent review runs, and the content-integrity check for completed plans left marked active. A new solution note captures how to test filesystem safety at the operation boundary, including FIFO substitution, bounded descriptor reads, metadata identity checks, and isolated fault injection.

Published 2026-09-10 · Updated 2026-09-10 · View on GitHub

What’s new

Section titled “What’s new”

This release adds an operator-facing cleanup path for ce:review artifacts, turns on noUncheckedIndexedAccess repo-wide, and converts a hand-measured eval-scanner coverage claim into a test that re-runs itself.

Features

Section titled “Features”

Review artifacts can now be cleaned up, and are ignored before they are written. Review runs retain private source excerpts indefinitely, with no supported way to age them out. The new ce:review-cleanup skill (#965) closes that gap with a deliberately conservative shape: a required age cutoff, a read-only preview, and a separate deletion approval bound to the previewed selection and that fixed cutoff. Before removal it rechecks directory identity, ancestry, and subtree metadata, rejects unsafe traversal, and reports partial failures instead of an all-clear. Complementing it, writable review runs now prepare .context/.gitignore with /systematic/ce-review/ before artifacts exist, preserving existing bytes; missing Git or ambiguous verification blocks persistence, and report-only mode remains no-write. Both ship as independent Node helpers alongside their owning skills, with strict argument handling and read-only usage help.

The safety boundaries are stated rather than implied. Age means the latest filesystem modification within a run, not proof that nothing is writing to it — the offline acknowledgment is an operator precondition, not a liveness check, and the preview token detects stale state without authenticating approval. There is no automatic expiry and no new source-redaction mode. Ignore rules do not protect tracked files, force-adds, or copies made elsewhere, and deletion is irreversible with no rollback or backup.

Documentation

Section titled “Documentation”

ARCHITECTURE.md and STRUCTURE.md caught up with three shipped changes (#960). Review artifact validation now documents the containment default and the --allow-outside-artifact-root escape hatch. Named model profiles gained a cross-cutting entry covering resolveActiveProfile, resolveProfileSelector, and the trust boundary: profiles sits in PROJECT_PROTECTED_FIELDS alongside workflow_guard, so a project systematic.json may select a profile but a profiles map it defines is ignored with a warning rather than merged. The host-contract gate is recorded too — the host-contract job, scripts/host-contract-guard.ts, and scripts/lib/opencode-pin.ts — including that it is a required predecessor of release and that evidence gathered at one pinned OpenCode version is not evidence at another. Every claim was checked against the code it describes.

A new learning records what counts as evidence for a “nothing changed” claim (#961). Two changes shipped the same defect an hour apart: one asserted no runtime behavior changed while reassigning an array OpenCode owns, and one claimed a project overlay could override profile-supplied routing when the code rejects rather than strips. Both were confident claims about the far side of a boundary, and both survived multi-persona review — eleven personas returned zero findings on the array conversion, because every existing test read the value back off the same object and so passed under either semantics. The rule the doc records: a no-change claim is scoped to a boundary, neither the diff nor a passing suite is evidence for it, and if the contract is real you pin it with a test that fails under the wrong semantics. It is indexed by symptom rather than by lesson, so the tags carry the identifiers actually involved.

Three shipped plans in docs/plans/ are marked completed (#957). Each unit was verified against the current tree rather than against the plan’s own prose, and half the reported drift turned out not to be drift — a program document and two genuinely incomplete plans were correctly left active, with reasons stated. content-integrity.ts now catches one narrow shape of this problem: a plan marked status: active whose units are all ticked fails the gate. Notably, it does not catch the drift this change fixed, since “shipped but nobody ticked a box” is indistinguishable from “not started” using frontmatter and checkboxes alone.

Tests

Section titled “Tests”

The eval fixture scanner re-proves its own coverage on every run (#958). The scanner’s blind spots had been measured by hand and quoted as a number at a commit — a technique nobody could re-run, so nothing re-checked it when the scanner or the files it reads changed. probeScannerBlindSpots now plants a version literal at every line position of every allowlisted fixture file and asserts the scanner reports it, across all four historical injection shapes, so a regression confined to one shape or one scanner code path cannot hide behind the others passing. Non-detections inside comments or inside an already-open template literal are classified as legitimate per shape, derived from the scanner’s own tokenizer output rather than a second hand-written walk over the source. The probe is itself proven: reconstructing each of the three prior scanner designs makes the sweep fail and name the positions each would have missed, and a deliberately crippled stub scanner produces a real miss. The stated limit is that the sweep re-proves detection only for the shapes and positions present in today’s files.

Code Refactoring

Section titled “Code Refactoring”

noUncheckedIndexedAccess is on, and all 132 surfaced sites are fixed (#959). z.record(z.string(), V) infers Record<string, V>, so parsed.categories.anything type-checked clean and threw at runtime — a trap that applied to every indexed read in the repo, not just the config schema. The flag now lives in the base tsconfig.json, inherited by the scripts and tests configs, with all sites fixed in the same commit because typecheck:all is a required gate and a partial fix would land red. One site changed observably and was corrected: an interim output.system = output.system.map(...) in applyBootstrapContent reassigned an array that a sibling hook captures by reference, which would have silently dropped injected bootstrap content; the loop now mutates in place and a test pins array identity across the call. Every other site was checked individually and is type-only, with four regression tests pinning the narrowings that landed on live branches. Consumers are unaffected — dist/lib/config-schema.d.ts is byte-identical with and without the flag.

The parsed config shape is inferred instead of erased (#955). createSystematicConfigSchema declared its return type as z.ZodObject<z.core.$ZodLooseShape>, which threw away the shape the schema actually parses; callers got a loose object, and the config test compensated with a hand-maintained ParsedSystematicConfig mirror plus a cast helper that nothing kept in sync. Removing the annotations lets the shape infer from the builders and deletes the mirror. Inference degrades gracefully here — record-keyed fields infer as Record<string, T> rather than expanding to literal keys, and typecheck:all stays clean at roughly the same speed. Ordinary toEqual assertions now fail to compile when the schema gains an unaccounted required field, though an added .optional() field with no default still drifts silently, and SystematicConfigParsed’s docstring records that scope. Because annotating a Zod schema builder erases its inferred shape, AGENTS.md and .github/copilot-instructions.md now record an explicit exception to the repo’s explicit-return-type convention.

Published 2026-09-08 · Updated 2026-09-08 · View on GitHub

What’s new

Section titled “What’s new”

Bug Fixes

Section titled “Bug Fixes”

Workflow guard replay keeps the original failure reason (#954). When a completion tool call was delivered twice for the same callID, two terminal outcomes lost their specific reason code on the second delivery: a mismatched completion target (invalid-transition) and a host-tool failure (failed-operation) both fell through to a generic guard-unavailable. Both branches now record a terminal completion and replay it with the reason code that produced it. The host-tool-failure record is flagged metadata-only, so a replay corrects the guard metadata without overwriting the host’s own failure title and output — that text is evidence and has to survive untouched.

Two related fidelity gaps closed alongside it. TerminalComplete.target is now optional, so a genuinely-unknown target is omitted from the emitted workflowGuard metadata rather than fabricated as unit. And stale questionAttestation stripping is now gated on the guard instance’s own sourceDigest, so two guard instances sharing an output reference can no longer erase each other’s attestation evidence. All three gaps were safety-neutral — the host failure sentinel survived in every case, and no fail-closed behaviour was weakened — but each degraded the accuracy of the completion evidence record the guard exists to protect.

Code Refactoring

Section titled “Code Refactoring”

The host-contract CI guard is now a tested script (#949). The host-contract job’s skip/pass guard lived as a ~135-line inline .mjs heredoc inside .github/workflows/main.yaml. It parsed JUnit XML and the bun test log with regexes and gated release — an untested parser sitting on a required release gate, invisible to biome check ., typecheck:all, and bun test. It now lives in scripts/host-contract-guard.ts as pure functions plus a thin CLI wrapper, with unit tests covering all five failure conditions, XML entity decoding, and the artifact-reading paths.

The move also fixed a gating bug that had survived two rounds of review. The guard step’s if: condition contained no status check function, so GitHub Actions applied its own implicit, job-scoped success() on top — skipping the guard on exactly the runs where its diagnosis matters most, a failing suite. Adding !cancelled() fixes it, and tests/unit/host-contract-workflow.test.ts now mechanically pins the condition’s properties so this class of regression fails a test instead of shipping a third time. A missing or unreadable artifact is now reported as the contract failure it is — routed through the same evaluate() path a truncated one already used — instead of a raw ENOENT crash.

Tests

Section titled “Tests”

A mis-detected quote can no longer blind the fixture-version scanner (#947). The scanner in tests/unit/opencode-pin.test.ts enforces that every OpenCode-shaped version literal in the allowlisted fixture files stays inside the unpinnable 9999.x sentinel range. Its tokenizer could misread an apostrophe inside a regex literal in an unrecognised position — if (a && /don't/.test(b)) — as an opening quote; the phantom string then searched forward for the next real quote and swallowed everything in between.

Rather than extend the regex-position heuristic for a third time, this applies a structural bound: a ' or " string cannot span a real newline in JS/TS, so the tokenizer abandons an unterminated span the moment it reaches a line break. That caps the damage from any mis-detected quote, whatever the trigger, to the rest of the current line. Backtick template literals are excluded, since they legitimately span newlines. Three regression tests pin each of the three historical hazards, and the plant-at-every-line-position probe reports zero genuine misses across all four scanned files.

Documentation

Section titled “Documentation”

How to measure a source scanner’s blind spots (#950). A new docs/solutions/best-practices/ entry records the lesson from that scanner work: a guard that scans source text has to have its blind spots measured, because reading it finds nothing. Three successive designs each read as correct and each had a measured hole — context-anchored matching missed the four literal shapes the scanned file actually used, a blanket match with a comment stripper went blind over 143 of 143 positions after a single // inside a string desynced quote parity, and removing comment awareness entirely missed 166–580 positions to a phantom string opened by an apostrophe in prose. The doc records the probe that found all three, the structural bound that caps any future mis-detection regardless of cause, and the cheap positive result: the same probe cleared the sibling guards in tests/unit/spawn-and-signal-conventions.test.ts at zero misses, so the technique validates as well as condemns.

v3.16.4…v3.16.5

v3.16.4

Section titled “v3.16.4”

Published 2026-09-07 · Updated 2026-09-07 · View on GitHub

What’s new

Section titled “What’s new”

One theme dominates this release: the OpenCode host contract stopped being a local ritual and became a required, fail-closed CI gate. A five-unit plan landed end to end (#916, #928, #930, #931, #937), and the very first real-host CI runs immediately caught four bugs sitting in already-merged code — each now pinned by a host-free regression test. In parallel, the typecheck:all backlog opened in #914 was burned all the way down: 343 errors across 30 files, to zero.

Bug Fixes

Section titled “Bug Fixes”

systematic_workflow_complete could report success while carrying stale evidence. The tool returns runtime.metadata() first, which may describe a ready-but-not-finalized unit (reasonCode: 'unit-ready', no workflowGuard block). Four branches in finishComplete()/finalizeComplete() returned without ever rewriting that output, so a completion the host marked completed was indistinguishable from a real success. Each branch now writes an explicit terminal result using the existing WorkflowReasonCode vocabulary — invalid-transition for a mismatched finalize target, guard-unavailable when nothing replayable is known, finalization-failed on an unavailable readback, and failed-operation when the host tool itself failed. No new status or reason literal was introduced, and the guard’s state-machine semantics are unchanged; only the evidence written to tool output changed.

Two follow-on defects surfaced during review of the same change and were fixed in it. The completion writers replaced output.metadata wholesale instead of layering onto it, dropping the host’s own failure sentinel on the shared output reference and letting a second guard instance take the success path. And metadata() emitted a bare, unprefixed status key whenever workflow_guard.debug was enabled, which still overwrote the host’s status: 'error' sentinel even after the layering fix — reintroducing the same fail-open through a user-settable option. That debug-only key is now debugEpochStatus, so it cannot collide with a host-owned status field in any mode. Seven bidirectional proofs back the change (#945).

Build System

Section titled “Build System”

The pinned OpenCode development dependency moved to v1.18.22 (#880). Because the host pin is now derived from package.json rather than hand-copied constants (see Code Refactoring below), a bump like this is a single-field edit that the host-contract job re-proves automatically.

Documentation

Section titled “Documentation”

Two solutions docs record what the host-contract work actually taught. host-contract-evidence-is-ci-owned-2026-09-04.md keeps the surviving invariant from the earlier 2026-08-16 doc — evidence gathered at one pinned OpenCode version is not evidence at another — and replaces the mechanism: the pin lives in package.json, the host is bunx opencode-ai@<pin>, and the evidence is the required host-contract job that release depends on. A Renovate OpenCode bump is now complete when that job is green on the PR; nobody re-runs the suite by hand. The superseded doc keeps its body as history with status: superseded frontmatter and a pointer to the replacement (#937).

The companion doc, real-host-ci-catches-what-offline-gates-cannot-2026-09-06.md, catalogues the bug classes only a real host can catch: four defects in merged code that passed unit tests, typecheck:all, lint, content-integrity, review, and offline skip runs, and were caught only by the new required job. It records the measured launcher topology on both macOS and Linux, two diagnostic traps, and the practice of pinning each host-caught bug with a host-free unit test (#938).

Tests

Section titled “Tests”

The real-host CI job found four bugs on its first runs, and this release fixes all of them.

A 180-second hang with zero output turned out to be stdio: spawnOpencodeChild used Node’s default spawn stdio, leaving stdin an open, unclosed pipe that a real opencode run blocks on waiting for EOF. Switching to stdio: ['ignore', 'pipe', 'pipe'] took the previously-hanging tests from a 180s kill to a ~25s pass. The same PR converted one remaining bare opencode spawn site — missed by the earlier bunx conversion — to bunx opencode-ai@<pin> (#932).

The full integration suite exited 130 (SIGINT) even though every individual test passed. process is a single process-wide emitter shared by every test file in a Bun worker, so one eval-runner test’s process.emit('SIGINT') reached the host fixture’s never-removed SIGINT safety net, which called process.exit(130) unconditionally. The synthetic signal is now isolated to the listener under test (#933).

A test asserting that the fixture’s launcher pid equals the pid the plugin reports from inside the OpenCode process passed on macOS and failed in CI with values exactly +1 apart. bunx execs the binary in place on macOS but forks it as a child on Linux, so the identity never held cross-platform. The test now asserts what it actually needs to prove — one probe load per host generation, in order (#936).

The fixture’s reaper failed open: isProcessGroupAlive() treated every error from process.kill(-pid, 0) as proof the group was gone, collapsing POSIX EPERM (“exists, not yours to signal”) into ESRCH (“gone”). That let the pruner drop a live entry and the SIGKILL sweep skip a still-running group, leaking a live opencode process past exit — a failure mode that previously caused a machine reboot on this project. It now returns false only for ESRCH and fails closed on everything else (#943).

A broader hardening pass on the host fixture’s spawn, stdio, and signal handling landed alongside these: pruneLiveOpencodeProcesses() re-probes and evicts stale pids on every check instead of relying on a one-shot eviction at settle time, multi-byte UTF-8 chunk reassembly is pinned by a test, and buildDetachedChildSpawnOptions is now the single shared spawn-options builder both spawn sites call through, so they cannot diverge on stdio (#941).

Two host-free source-scan guards now pin the bug classes CI caught, so they cannot regress silently: one rejects any spawn call whose first argv element is the literal 'opencode', the other rejects any process.emit of a terminal signal anywhere under tests/ (#939).

The rest of the Tests bucket is the typecheck:all burn-down against #897, which finished in this release. The four highest-error test files accounted for 195 of the 343 baseline errors and went to zero by narrowing discriminated-union results behind explicit helpers, giving fixture builders real return types instead of Record<string, unknown>, and correcting a wrong-module type import (#919). Three real-host integration files adopted a per-file unwrapData() helper rather than reading the SDK’s {data?, error?} response wrapper unguarded (#922). The eval fixture factories and case unions were typed against the real EvalResult, SourceProvenance, and CaseId exports (#923). Six unit files got complete SDK-shaped Model fixtures, ToolResult union narrowing, and type guards in place of runtime-only assertions (#924). The final batch took the count from 55 to zero, with the only source-side changes being additive: exporting CapabilityCliRoots, and adding a narrow read helper for the skill permission map that config-handler.ts genuinely writes but the imported v1 Config type omits (#926). No assertion behaviour changed anywhere in the burn-down.

Separately, the last two mkdtempSync cleanup gaps in the unit suite were closed — agent-resolver and pi-delegate-session were leaving 19 orphaned temp directories per run (#918).

Continuous Integration

Section titled “Continuous Integration”

The headline change is a required host-contract job that runs tests/integration against a real, bunx-launched OpenCode host and gates release. It builds dist/ before testing (load-bearing: the dist-local assertion is computed at module scope, so a late build would silently skip it), sets SYSTEMATIC_REQUIRE_OPENCODE=1 in workflow-owned env that a fork PR cannot alter, and always runs to completion so it is a valid required check. Path gating lives at step level and fails closed on any unexpected filter output. A JUnit-parsing guard then refuses to pass unless every one of the eleven integration files produced at least one test suite, the skipped set matches the known-exempt set exactly, and the pass count clears a floor — so “green with everything skipped” is not reachable (#931).

The wider type check landed as a staged rollout: typecheck:scripts covering src/, scripts/, and docs/scripts/ as a required step with no backlog, and typecheck:all covering tests/ too as advisory (continue-on-error: true) so the then-343-error backlog could surface without gating merges (#914).

The Node ESM load probe now covers dist/cli.js. package.json declares bin.systematic -> ./dist/cli.js, but the probe only imported dist/index.js and dist/pi.js — so a bare specifier that resolves under Bun but not plain Node would have shipped an unloadable systematic bin with no CI signal. This is not hypothetical: another project shipped exactly that failure from a bare jsonc-parser import resolving to a UMD main, and Systematic imports jsonc-parser bare in src/lib/setup.ts and src/lib/config.ts. The probe asserts loadability only, since dist/cli.js legitimately exports named symbols (#940).

Code Refactoring

Section titled “Code Refactoring”

The pinned OpenCode host version now has one readable source. scripts/lib/opencode-pin.ts reads the @opencode-ai/sdk devDependency from package.json, resolved relative to the module rather than cwd, and throws a clear error naming the field if it is missing or not an exact version. The two hand-maintained constants in scripts/run-evals.ts and the integration fixture became re-exports of it, retiring a four-way lockstep (#916).

Every host the suite spawns now launches through bunx opencode-ai@<pin> instead of npx, with no PATH lookup. A new probeOpencodeAvailability classifies a host as available, mismatch (exit 0 at the wrong version), or unavailable, and requireOpencodeAvailable turns a bad classification into a module-scope throw when SYSTEMATIC_REQUIRE_OPENCODE=1. Critically, the fixture module itself probes nothing at module scope, so tests/unit importers never spawn bunx. The shared bun install cache directory is resolved with lstat on every call — never stat, which would follow a planted symlink — and is refused outright if it is a symlink, not a directory, or not owned by the current uid (#928).

The host model test’s last network dependency is gone. runOpencode now starts a local OpenAI-compatible scripted model server per invocation and merges its provider config into the fixture’s isolated config, dispatching on request-body shape rather than call order — OpenCode forks a background title-generation call concurrently with the main chat loop, so ordering assumptions do not hold. All seven call sites were left untouched because the scripted-provider logic lives entirely inside runOpencode. The same change deleted the suite’s only unfalsifiable test, which asserted that a cell status was one of two values that covered every possible outcome (#930).

What’s new

Section titled “What’s new”

A maintenance release: the review-artifact validator can now check artifacts that live outside a live run directory, the Fro Bot autoheal workflow actually lands its file changes instead of discarding them, and the plan corpus was refreshed.

Bug Fixes

Section titled “Bug Fixes”

validate-review-artifact gains a --allow-outside-artifact-root flag, wired into both the standalone CLI (src/cli.ts) and the bundled Claude Code validator entry (src/claude-code-validator.ts). Previously the resolved path had to stay inside .context/systematic/ce-review, and that directory had to exist — which meant an artifact fetched from CI, attached to an issue, or checked in as a fixture could not be validated without first being copied into a live run directory. The flag drops both requirements.

Every other guarantee stays enforced regardless of the flag: lexical .. traversal rejection, symlink rejection on every path component, realpath canonicalization before the file check, a regular-file check on the resolved target, and the no-echo guarantee that error output never contains the supplied path or file contents. Argument parsing, the usage string, and the flag constant were hoisted into src/lib/review-artifact-path.ts — the module both entries already shared for path resolution — so the two command surfaces are the same code rather than hand-maintained copies. The flag is idempotent, and a successful external-mode validation prints a distinct message so a transcript cannot mistake it for the current run’s evidence.

The synthesis artifact contract doc records the flag as an external-validation mode with an explicit warning: the ce:review parent must never pass it when validating its own run’s review-summary.json, since that would silently accept a mismatched or misplaced artifact as that run’s evidence (#915, 690a7f1).

Continuous Integration

Section titled “Continuous Integration”

The Fro Bot workflow now requests branch-pr delivery for autoheal runs, so the daily autoheal cron and prompt-less autoheal dispatches land their file changes on a branch instead of discarding them. The gate mirrors the PROMPT ladder directly above it, and a test pins that the two expressions agree. Because inputs.mode defaults to autoheal, the inputs.prompt == '' guard is what keeps prompt-only dispatches — such as the release-notes narrative automation in scripts/dispatch-release-notes.sh — comment-only. PR-review, comment, workflow_call, and review-mode runs resolve to the empty string and keep their current behavior.

The autoheal prompt’s code-quality list and quality-gates table now cover all four drift gates: review-schema:drift and agent-browser:drift join the existing registry:drift and schema:drift, with new assertions in tests/unit/fro-bot-workflow.test.ts. Delivery still depends on FRO_BOT_PAT scopes — an insufficient token fails closed to the previous discard behavior, so the first scheduled run’s resolved-output-mode is worth checking (#912, 5f38bb9).

Documentation

Section titled “Documentation”

A new plan covers a CI gate that resolves every shipped model identifier — OMO profile routing, config-schema.ts examples, hand-written docs, and skill-reference examples — against a committed snapshot of the models.dev registry, plus a refresh script with a drift check and a weekly workflow that opens a PR when the registry changes. A retired identifier then fails that PR’s gate by name; nothing rewrites routing choices. The gate is planned to live inside content-integrity as a hard, offline pass/fail so main.yaml gains no new step, and schema examples are read from the same Zod producer that emits the published JSON Schema rather than by parsing TypeScript (#908, a0ccd3b).

Three shipped plans were marked completed — the review-artifact executable contract fix, the review-artifact contract refactor, and the OpenCode plugin load-failure fix — taking the active plan census from 10 down to 7 (#911, 58ece67).

A small patch release: one runtime dependency bump and one expansion of the solutions corpus around deletion and preservation gates.

Bug Fixes

Section titled “Bug Fixes”

web-tree-sitter moves from 0.26.12 to 0.27.0. This is a production dependency rather than a dev tool — it is the WASM parser runtime behind the receipt classifier in src/lib/receipt-classifier.ts, and it stays version-pinned and Renovate-grouped with tree-sitter-bash because the runtime and the grammar have to move together. Documentation

Section titled “Documentation”

The deletion-gate learning doc (deletion-gates-must-observe-every-field-the-deleted-code-wrote-2026-08-16.md) gains the sign-flipped case found while landing #903: a preservation gate — a corpus meant to prove that a rewrite still matches the code it replaced — is only as complete as the deleted code’s branches, not just the fields that code wrote.

The concrete failure is the useful part. The variant-clearing heuristic that the doc already named as a live regression target was replaced by the routing resolver in #903. Its twelve-entry compatibility corpus had been seeded from existing fixtures, and none of those fixtures set a category variant and then overrode model at the agent level. The rewrite consequently dropped two of the heuristic’s three branches and still passed byte-for-byte. Two rows built directly from the heuristic’s own conditions — corpus entries 013 and 014, with expected output captured from pre-change main — were what actually caught it.

The update adds a Guidance subsection covering the three-branch heuristic, why fixture-seeded corpora systematically miss deleted branches, and a three-step procedure for enumerating those branches; an Examples table mapping input to pre-change output to the rewrite’s output as it behaved before those rows existed; and refreshed frontmatter (last_updated, two new tags, two new applies_when entries, all within schema limits). It landed as an update to the existing doc rather than a new one — overlap scored High on all five dimensions, sharing the same deleted code, the same root cause (a gate derived from something other than the deleted code itself), the same enumerate-from-git show remedy, and the same files, with the prevention rule generalised from fields to branches. (#905)

What’s new

Section titled “What’s new”

Features

Section titled “Features”

Named model profiles with per-harness routing blocks (#903) — User config can now define named profiles, and any config source, including a repository’s project config, can select one by name. Agent and category overlays gain optional per-harness blocks — opencode: { model, variant } and pi: { model, thinking } — so a single systematic.jsonc routes correctly on both OpenCode and Pi. One routing resolver feeds the OpenCode config hook, the Pi delegate tool, Pi persona export, and systematic config show.

Resolution is layered and predictable. The profile selector follows source strength (OPENCODE_CONFIG_DIR > project > user) and is tri-state, so null explicitly selects the base config. Overlays merge user base, then the selected profile, then the project’s permitted fields, then custom; per target per harness the precedence is agent block, agent flat, category block, category flat. An unknown profile name warns once and falls back to the user’s own default rather than base — a repository can never push a contributor off the routing they chose.

The trust boundary holds: project config may select a profile but never define one. profiles coming from project config is stripped with a warning, and model, variant, and thinking inside harness blocks are rejected from project config exactly like the flat fields already were.

One behaviour change is worth noting. A flat agents.<name>.model now routes Pi delegates too; previously it was OpenCode-only and Pi always inherited the parent model. The first dispatch of a config-routed agent says so in the tool result, naming the model, its source, and the active profile. pi_subagents.<name>.thinking is superseded by agents.<name>.pi.thinking, with the old location still working when the new one is absent and emitting one deprecation warning per written field. Every pre-existing configuration produces byte-identical OpenCode agent config, asserted byte-for-byte against a fourteen-configuration corpus.

Alongside the resolver, systematic config show now reports the active profile, its source, any fallback, and per-agent routing per harness, with --json emitting the same information as a single object. Claude Code routing, fallback_models chains, and shipping the OMO registry routing as a named profile remain out of scope.

Documentation

Section titled “Documentation”

The OpenCode host-contract suite now has a plan for becoming CI-owned (#898). Today the integration tests that spawn OpenCode assert real host mechanics — plugin loading, config-hook merge, tool registration, system-prompt transforms, question API shapes, receipt persistence across restart — but none of it runs in CI, and the only automated effect of the version pin is a unit test that goes red on every Renovate OpenCode bump until someone re-runs a 15–17 minute suite locally. The plan makes package.json’s @opencode-ai/sdk the single pin read at runtime, launches every host through bunx opencode-ai@<pin>, and adds a host-contract CI job that is a required predecessor of release with a post-run guard so a green job cannot simply be a run of skipped suites.

ARCHITECTURE.md and STRUCTURE.md were also synced to the bundled validator work (#894): the Claude Code plugin build section now documents that bin/ entries are written with executable mode and that the CI pre-publish guard asserts the bundled validator is executable rather than merely present, and the brittle unit-test file counts were refreshed.

Tests

Section titled “Tests”

The Claude Code integration suite now builds the real validator bundle (#895). That suite had been failing on main since the bundled validator landed: generatePluginFiles gained a required validator Buffer argument and the integration suite still called it with one argument, throwing at module load before any test ran. buildValidatorBundle is now exported and built once per module load, both call sites pass it, and a new assertion checks that the generated bin/systematic-validate-review-artifact is exactly one shebang line followed by the bundle bytes. A second latent failure — agent stem discovery picking up agents/review/README.md, which the build already excludes — was hidden behind the original error and is fixed too.

Integration runs also stop leaking OpenCode servers (#896). Both host spawn sites launched through a launcher chain and stopped only the direct child, so the server outlived every failed, timed-out, or aborted run until the machine had to be rebooted. Hosts now spawn detached in their own process group and are reaped with SIGTERM, a five-second wait, then SIGKILL of the group; startup-timeout cleanup is awaited before the failure surfaces; and a suite-level registry of live hosts is drained in afterAll so a test that aborts before its own finally still leaves nothing behind. Availability probing switched from which to running opencode --version under a throwaway HOME/XDG root, so a shim that only resolves through the redirected HOME makes the suite skip instead of spawning servers that cannot start.

What’s new

Section titled “What’s new”

A maintenance release whose one substantive change closes a drift gap in the dependency-update pipeline: artifacts that are generated from a dependency now regenerate inside the Renovate branch that bumps it, so a schema-affecting upgrade lands complete rather than red.

Bug Fixes

Section titled “Bug Fixes”

Zod moves from 4.4.3 to 4.5.4 (#891, 4e99f0e). The upgrade changes the JSON Schema that Zod emits for ISO date-time fields: the date-time pattern in skills/ce-review/references/review-summary-schema.json now requires an explicit seconds component instead of treating it as optional. Because that file is checked in and generated from Zod’s toJSONSchema output, the regenerated schema travels in the same commit as the bump — the first Renovate PR to exercise the post-upgrade wiring described below. The same PR also carries typebox to 1.3.24.

If you validate ce:review summary payloads against the published schema, completed_at values must now include seconds (2026-09-04T17:52:51Z), not just hours and minutes.

Continuous Integration

Section titled “Continuous Integration”

Renovate regenerates every dependency-derived artifact, not just one (#893, aff01fe). The postupgrade script that Renovate runs in-branch previously covered only bun run build and the agent-browser stub regeneration. It now also runs schema:generate, review-schema:generate, and scripts/generate-registry.ts.

The gap stayed invisible until a bump hit it: an update that shifted the config schema, the review-summary schema, or registry content would open a PR that failed its own drift gates, and a human had to regenerate the file by hand before the update could merge. Extending postUpgradeTasks moves that work into the branch that caused it. The Zod bump above is the immediate proof — its regenerated schema arrived inside the update PR instead of as a follow-up fix.

Documentation

Section titled “Documentation”

A stated merge order is not an enforced one (#874, dd32db0). A new learning in docs/solutions/workflow-issues/ records a pull request that stated the precondition it then failed to satisfy: its body said to merge a dependency first, explained precisely why, and was based on a commit that predated it — leaving it mergeable in exactly the order it warned against. The warning was accurate and completely inert. The reviewer caught it only by building the artifact at that branch’s head and finding that the command the prose told readers to run was not executable.

The doc gives equal weight to the alternative, because stacking had failed the same day: a pull request opened against another open pull request’s branch lost its base when that branch merged and was deleted, and creation failed outright. Being burned by that is what produced the retreat to prose, which felt safer and was strictly weaker. So the guidance is conditional rather than a slogan — stack when the dependency is not about to merge and let the platform refuse the wrong order; hold the dependent branch unopened when the dependency is approved and could land at any moment; write the dependency down as well, but never only that. Recovery from a vanished base is documented too, since knowing it is cheap makes the stacking risk feel correctly sized.

Both failures share a cause: the ordering lived somewhere that could not enforce it. Of the two, the description is worse — a vanished base fails loudly and immediately, while a description fails by saying nothing at all.

What’s new

Section titled “What’s new”

This release closes the loop on the Claude Code review-artifact validator: it now ships as a real, executable command inside the plugin bundle instead of prose describing one that couldn’t run, and the contract that names it has been corrected to describe how the parent actually reaches it.

Features

Section titled “Features”

The Claude Code bundle had shipped prose naming a validate-review-artifact command with nothing able to run it, so validation there recorded an absence rather than a result (#871). It now carries a real executable — bin/systematic-validate-review-artifact, built in memory at bundle time and reachable as a bare command. Containment helpers moved out of the CLI into their own module: the CLI’s import graph reaches the JSONC config loader, and a bundle that pulls that in builds cleanly but dies at runtime looking for a module its own wrapper requires by name. Exporting from the CLI would have reintroduced exactly that defect. The entry imports only the schema and the extracted helpers, keeping it at 0.28 MB with nothing resolved at runtime, and reproduces the subcommand’s behavior exactly — including the projection that reports only field paths and error codes so artifact contents never reach the output. A companion refactor consolidated three functions and a type that had been duplicated byte-for-byte between the CLI and the bundled validator, closing the risk that one copy could quietly regain a legacy-artifact classification bug already caught once in review. Verified by running the built artifact from outside the repository against valid, invalid, legacy, malformed, and missing inputs, and confirming a planted marker in every string field of an invalid artifact never leaked into the output.

The bundle writer had been creating every file with a default mode, so the validator shipped without an executable bit and could only run via an interpreter named in front of it — defeating the point of living in a bin directory (#872). Entries under bin are now written executable; nothing else changes mode, since restoring source modes across the whole bundle would be a broader change with no demand behind it. The pre-publish guard also gained this check, now asserting the entry is executable rather than merely present — presence alone wouldn’t catch a file that exists, passes every other check, and still can’t run. Verified by copying the built entry outside the repository with its mode preserved and running it directly with no interpreter: valid, invalid, legacy, malformed, and missing inputs all returned their documented codes, and removing then restoring the bit confirmed the guard catches both directions.

Documentation

Section titled “Documentation”

skills/ce-review/references/synthesis-artifact-contract.md told the parent to look for one command on PATH and warned that a harness installing only bundled markdown wouldn’t have it — true when written, false now that the Claude Code bundle ships its own validator beside the prose naming it (#873). The revised passage states the resolution order explicitly: the bundled command first, then the packaged subcommand. It also directs callers to run the command rather than test for its presence, since a name on PATH can be a shim that fails on every invocation — a documented failure elsewhere in this repository — so resolving a name proves nothing that running it doesn’t prove better. Absent and present-but-broken stay distinct: both record the run as unavailable, but neither is ever a failed validation, since that value means an artifact was read and did not conform. Two learnings that had asserted the bundle carries no executable were corrected; the recommendations they made survive untouched. A companion change marked the bundled-validator plan complete, since all five units had shipped across three pull requests but the plan still read as though none had.
