What’s new

Section titled “What’s new”

A small documentation-heavy release: one scoring fix in the compound workflow’s related-docs step, plus four docs that trace a costly false assumption from discovery to correction.

Bug Fixes

Section titled “Bug Fixes”

skills: derive the overlap score from the dimension count (#870)

The compound workflow’s related-docs step scores how similar a proposed learning is to an existing one across five named dimensions, and that score decides whether a session writes a new document or updates an existing one. The scoring logic got this decision wrong four times in one session, in two distinct ways: the score was judged as a holistic read of “how related do these feel” rather than a literal count of matched dimensions, letting a report score two documents as near-duplicates while recommending a new document be written in the same breath; and the document search couldn’t find work clustered under a shared module, because it took its search term from keywords in the problem description rather than from the actual curated module identifiers in use. Both are fixed: the dimension count now reads directly into the score, with the count stated in the returned assessment — when the two disagree, the count wins — and the module search now enumerates the real module values in use and picks the closest match. A companion fix also separates the score-follows-count and recommendation-follows-score checks, which a prior read had collapsed into a single rule, obscuring which one had actually failed.

Documentation

Section titled “Documentation”

Four documentation changes landed, spanning solution captures and plan corrections that all trace back to one costly false premise.

Two solution docs record the lesson from a session where a plan was designed around an assumption that was never tested. The Claude Code plugin bundle was assumed unable to carry an executable, so an MCP server, a runtime version floor bump, a launch pin, and a new dependency were designed, reviewed by six personas, and merged as a plan — all before a single local install proved the premise false. A marketplace install actually copies the entire plugin directory, including files the manifest never declares, with the executable bit intact and bin/ already on the Bash tool’s PATH; no transport is needed to reach a bundled executable (#869). That doc captures the general lesson — a working capability that has never had its cause isolated hasn’t proven anything; remove the suspected cause and re-run to confirm — and links it to an existing five-week-old rule about probing unproven runtime channels before designing around them. A second doc records the specific anchor convention now required in every fenced script block: skills that invoked helper scripts with bare relative paths resolved against the consumer’s working directory rather than the skill’s install directory, breaking on every harness. The fix is three rules: every block (not just the file) must (re)set the anchor, the assignment must use a form that terminates correctly even when a host flattens a fenced block to one line, and the anchor stays model-filled rather than sourced from a host variable, since a substitution offered by one harness silently expands to nothing on the others (#866).

The two plan documents in this release close out that same story. The MCP server plan is marked superseded, since its central assumption — that a Claude Code bundle can’t carry an executable — was never measured and turned out to be false; the real constraint is entry-point scope, since the full CLI can’t be bundled (a jsonc-parser UMD branch requires runtime resolution the bundler can’t do statically), but a narrower entry importing only the review-artifact schema builds to a self-contained file. The plan stays in place behind a status banner rather than being deleted, pointing at the measurements that replaced it (#867). In its place, a new plan describes building a review-artifact validator that ships as an in-bundle executable, with every claim it depends on — the install copies undeclared directories, the executable bit survives, the entry is reachable as a bare shell command, confirmed via negative control — measured against a real install rather than assumed from documentation (#868). A follow-up correction to that plan notes that the claimed containment helper imports don’t actually exist yet as exports; extracting resolveReviewArtifactPath, hasParentDirectoryTraversal, and pathContainsSymlink from src/cli.ts is a prerequisite the file list should call out rather than assume.

What’s new

Section titled “What’s new”

Bug Fixes

Section titled “Bug Fixes”

Five bundled skills invoked helper scripts with bare relative paths — things like bash references/resolve-base.sh — which a shell resolves against the working directory (the user’s project) rather than the directory the skill was actually installed into. These invocations could never work, in any repository, including this one. Each call now resolves through a SKILL_DIR variable set from the directory the harness reports when the skill loads, with every fenced block setting the variable itself since blocks are copied and run independently. A follow-up fix closed a related gap where some hosts flatten a fenced block into a single line: an unterminated SKILL_DIR="..." assignment then collapses into the env-var-prefix form, causing the shell to expand the variable from the outer scope before the assignment takes effect and reproducing the same broken path by a different route. All twenty anchors now terminate correctly, and a new test covers the four properties these invocations depend on (#862).

A persona that omits the tools frontmatter field is not equally restricted across harnesses: on Pi it resolves to a read-only set (read, grep, find, ls), but on OpenCode the same omission means no restriction at all, because the comma-separated string form isn’t the map shape OpenCode expects and is silently ignored. Two personas were caught by this divergence with their capabilities backwards relative to their jobs — the PR comment resolver (which is supposed to implement fixes) and the bug reproduction validator (whose entire purpose is running reproductions) both effectively had no working tools declared. Both personas now explicitly declare the tools their instructions already assume. Granting shell access to the validator also required a new untrusted-input rule, since its input is a bug report — text that routinely arrives pasted from an issue tracker or a stranger’s terminal — and instructions embedded in that text must never be treated as instructions to the agent (#861).

Documentation

Section titled “Documentation”

A proposal to add an MCP server to the Claude Code bundle, premised on the bundle having no way to execute anything, was disproven by a local install: the install copies the whole plugin tree rather than only the manifest-declared components, preserves the executable bit, and bin/ reaches the Bash tool’s PATH. The real constraint turned out to be packaging, not execution — shipping the existing CLI failed three separate ways (a sibling-chunk import, externalized runtime dependencies with no node_modules to resolve them, and a UMD module with an AMD branch that no bundler can follow). An entry point that imports only the single module the surface needs avoids all three failure modes. The learning captured here: an unshippable dependency may have arrived through entry-point scope rather than through the feature being shipped, and is worth checking before being written off as fatal (#865).

Adding a module under src/lib/ has always carried two registration obligations, but only the ARCHITECTURE.md codemap was documented — the src/lib/AGENTS.md module table is equally required and equally gate-enforced (checkCodemapCompleteness and checkLibModuleTableCompleteness in scripts/content-integrity.ts). The guidance now names both obligations and the verification command, and points the intentional-omission escape hatch at whichever document the exclusion actually belongs to, rather than assuming the codemap (#863).

What’s new

Bug Fixes

Section titled “Bug Fixes”

ce-plan’s plan template records an origin field pointing at the brainstorm requirements document a plan was built from. Some repositories deliberately don’t track that directory, treating requirements as local planning input the plan itself supersedes — which meant every plan generated from such a repo carried a link that resolved to nothing once cloned elsewhere. The field itself is correct to keep: it preserves real provenance for whoever wrote the plan, and dropping it in favor of a second, equally-authoritative document just creates staleness the moment the plan lands. What was missing was a way for a reader to distinguish context they’re missing from context that was never shared in the first place. The Sources entry now states explicitly when the origin path is untracked, and the field contract documents why that’s a legitimate state rather than a broken link. The deepening pass previously assumed the origin file would always be readable; it now falls back to continuing from the plan alone and records that the fidelity check couldn’t run, instead of reporting a missing file (#860).

Documentation

Section titled “Documentation”

A new solutions note captures a diagnostic lesson from an incident where three dependency upgrades failed simultaneously and two were initially misdiagnosed from version numbers alone. The tree-sitter runtime failure looked like a grammar/ABI mismatch — the grammar trails the runtime by a minor version, peers pin the older range, and both were locked to the same line — but it was actually a renamed WASM asset; loading the pinned grammar under the new runtime confirmed the ABI was never involved. What obscured the real cause is that the command classifier fails closed: every shell classification came back unavailable, so forty-four assertions reported a classification result rather than surfacing a missing file, meaning the component was accurately describing its own state while saying nothing about the underlying cause. The third failure, a YAML dependency bump, looked like an ESM-only migration but the package still ships both formats — only the default export was removed — and because the importing module is the most depended-on file in the tree, the breakage fanned out across packaging, module resolution, and codegen in a way that reflected centrality rather than severity (#858).

What’s new

Build System

Section titled “Build System”

This release lands two dependency-maintenance changes that both required real verification work rather than a rubber-stamped version bump.

OpenCode was updated to v1.18.21 (#856). Renovate had proposed v1.18.19, but moving the OpenCode pin invalidates the evidence gathered at the old version and costs a seventeen-minute suite run against the real host — landing one patch behind current would mean paying that cost twice to catch up, so this bump goes straight to the latest published version instead. Four places have to agree or a guard fails: both OpenCode devDependencies, the expected version in the eval runner, and the exact version in the receipt workflow fixture. The version-dependent suite was re-run at 1.18.21 rather than assumed — fifty-one tests pass across the eval runner, artifact, and fixture files.

The tree-sitter runtime and grammar dependencies were grouped into a single change (#857). web-tree-sitter is the WASM runtime and tree-sitter-bash is the grammar it loads; a grammar is compiled against an ABI version and the runtime accepts a range, so moving one without the other can land the pair outside that range. Both are pinned exactly rather than with a caret for that reason, but nothing had previously stopped them from being proposed separately. The risk became concrete when the 0.26 bump renamed the runtime’s exported WASM file, breaking every call site that resolved the old name — the command classifier fails closed, so forty-four tests failed without a single parse having been attempted, and the fix belonged in the same change as the bump. Grouping these dependencies means that class of change now arrives as one reviewable PR instead of a half that cannot pass on its own.

Updated the web-tree-sitter dependency to v0.26.12, which surfaced a real regression rather than being a routine bump. The new runtime renamed the WASM asset it exports, from tree-sitter.wasm to web-tree-sitter.wasm, and three places in the codebase still asked for the old filename — so grammar resolution failed before the parser was ever initialized. Because the command classifier fails closed, every shell operation it needed to classify came back unavailable and minted no evidence, and forty-four tests failed without a single parse having been attempted. The grammar itself was never the problem: tree-sitter-bash 0.25.1 declares ABI 15, and the 0.26.12 runtime accepts ABI 13 through 15, so the pinned grammar continues to parse real commands correctly once the asset reference points at the renamed file. Drafted a plan for an MCP server in the Claude Code bundle. Systematic reaches Claude Code as markdown only, so bundled prose that names the command line tool can’t be satisfied there — Anthropic documents two ways a plugin can reach executable capability, and the current bundle uses neither, making the gap a build choice rather than a limit of the harness. The plan adds a stdio server declared in the bundle and launched on enable, exposing review artifact validation as a callable tool, sequenced across six units so the server exists before anything references it. Two findings reshaped the plan along the way: the validation path anchors its containment root to the process working directory, and a server started by the harness doesn’t have the project as its working directory, so every validation would have failed silently without adjustment; and the published package version at rest is a placeholder, so the launch reference has to come from the release job rather than the manifest. What’s new

Section titled “What’s new”

Small, focused release: the review artifact contract can now say exactly why a validation didn’t run, and a solutions doc that quoted the old, unconditional version of that instruction has been corrected.

Features

Section titled “Features”

ce-review: Unrun validations in the review artifact now record exactly where and why. Previously the contract told the parent to note that a validation didn’t run, without saying where that note should live — neighboring rules in the same file name their fields, so this one read as an instruction with nowhere to land (#853).

The run artifact now carries a validation object with an explicit status: passed, failed, unavailable, or not_attempted. A reason is required for the three non-passing states and rejected for passed, since a check that succeeded has nothing to explain and the field shouldn’t invite narration. The object deliberately does not reuse the existing coverage object — a validator_failures list already lives there and refers to the per-finding validation pass, a different mechanism that happens to share the word “validation.” Keeping them apart is the point of the change.

The status is self-reported: an agent can claim passed without having run anything, so this is not evidence that validation happened. What it buys is that four outcomes which previously produced one identical silence can now be told apart.

A follow-up commit tightened the documentation itself: the paragraph wiring the unavailable status to its trigger left the not_attempted case to inference, using the word “skipped” twice without ever pairing it with the status name. Both trigger conditions now name their status explicitly where the distinction is drawn.

Documentation

Section titled “Documentation”

A learning captured in docs/solutions/ describing the review artifact contract had gone stale the day after it was written. The note quoted the unconditional form of the validator instruction as the shipped design — but that instruction was corrected a day later, after it reached a harness with no executable to run (#852).

Two passages were wrong. The worked example told a reader to run the validator command outright, and the honest-limitation passage repeated the claim that an agent producing no evidence is an acceptable outcome, without the distinction the contract now draws between an agent choosing not to run a check and being unable to. The packaging section also gains the half the incident exposed: getting the validator into a reachable location is not the same as every reader of the contract being able to invoke it — bundled prose is copied into all three harness packages, while the bin entry only reaches installs of the npm package. An instruction naming a command has a wider reach than the command itself.

Bug Fixes

The ce-review synthesis contract told the parent agent to run a validator after writing the run artifact, with no condition attached to whether that validator existed. That instruction shipped verbatim into the Claude Code bundle, which is built without npm coupling and carries no executable at all — so an operator there was told to run something that cannot exist. The failure mode was silent in the worst available way: the same section said an agent that never runs the command produces no evidence either way, making an impossible command and a skipped one indistinguishable in the record. The instruction now states the condition under which the validator is reachable and says what to record when it is not, so unavailable and skipped are no longer conflated (#851).

Documentation

Section titled “Documentation”

A learning written on 16 August had already named the exact reason the review dedup fingerprint cannot match two reviewers describing one defect. An issue was filed against that same fingerprint on 20 August with the wrong cause, and the right cause was worked out again from scratch on 23 August — the answer had been sitting in docs/solutions the whole time. It was unfindable: its frontmatter read module: measurement with tags about evidence and instrument validation, naming neither the skill it came from nor the algorithm it described. Someone debugging deduplication searches for deduplication, not for an epistemics lesson they haven’t learned yet. The fix splits the two jobs — the title and body carry the general lesson, the frontmatter carries the particulars someone would actually search for — adding three tags to the older note was enough to make it reachable without disturbing its framing. It also fixes the knowledge-track template, which still listed four problem types after four more were added, and syncs the copy the refresh skill keeps (#850).

Bug Fixes

Section titled “Bug Fixes”

ce-review: The risk-aware degraded verdict in code review dispatch used to block unless another persona “covered the same surface” — a judgement call with no formal definition, so identical diffs and identical review findings could pass or block depending on who read them. Four independent reviewers of the change that introduced the rule ran into exactly this ambiguity.

The fix keeps signal that was already being computed and discarded: Stage 3 dispatch selection already determines and announces why each conditional persona was chosen, naming the endpoint or migration that triggered it. That reasoning is now recorded on the dispatch alongside the changed files, and “coverage” becomes a mechanical test — a validated finding covers a lost surface when its file is one of the recorded paths. A blocked verdict now states what would clear it (re-run the lost persona, or supply a validated finding on one of the recorded paths), and the verdict cites the specific finding that satisfied coverage so the decision can be reproduced from the artifact instead of taken on trust (#847).

A follow-up refactor in the same change widened the risk-critical persona-name tuple from an asserted cast to readonly string[], removing a type assertion that claimed an arbitrary string was one of five literals without anything actually checking it. Behavior is unchanged — all five risk-critical personas still require a selection surface, and always-on personas still do not.

Published 2026-08-23 · Updated 2026-08-23 · View on GitHub

What’s new

Section titled “What’s new”

Bug Fixes

Section titled “Bug Fixes”

ce-review: Finding deduplication was keyed on a fingerprint that included each finding’s normalized title. Because two reviewers rarely phrase the same finding the same way, the fingerprint almost never matched, so near-duplicate findings from independent reviewers passed through as separate results instead of being merged.

Measuring stored review runs quantified the problem: across twenty runs there were 375 cross-reviewer pairs of findings on the same file — 55 of them within three lines of each other and 39 on the exact same line — and none of them ever merged. That means the confidence boost meant to fire when independent reviewers converge on the same issue had never actually fired.

Line proximity was never the real signal, and prose files weren’t a special case either. Grouping is now mechanical and file-only, and the decision about whether two findings describe the same underlying defect is left to judgement — the one thing the model running this stage is actually good at. Declining to merge two findings is now recorded along with a reason: a wrong merge is obvious to a reader, but a missed merge just looks like two separate findings, so recording the decision either way leaves a trace.

A follow-up commit clarified how a partially-merged candidate group is recorded: when a group of three findings has two that merge and a third that doesn’t, one entry is written per declined separation, naming the IDs on both sides of it — so a three-finding group with a partial merge produces a single entry listing all three. A group that merges completely produces no declined-separation entries at all.

Bug Fixes

The ce:review contract specified writing a metadata.json file alongside the review summary, capturing the run ID, branch, HEAD, harness, verdict, and completion time — but no run had ever written it, and nothing in the repository read it. The instructions even described downstream skills falling back to file mtime when the file was absent, documentation for a consumer that was never built.

Investigation found that half of the contract had already collapsed on its own: the run artifact’s schema already carries run_id, harness, and verdict, and every real artifact on disk includes a verdict despite the (unwritten) contract placing that field elsewhere. Only branch, HEAD, and the completion timestamp were still homeless, so this fix moves those three fields into the artifact that is actually produced and validated (#842, 476a3b6).

The distinction the original design was reaching for still holds: branch and HEAD are captured at dispatch time, before any autofix lands, while the run artifact is written after the verdict is final — so a reader can tell whether the recorded state describes the checkout in front of them. Only the destination changed, not the semantics.

An earlier attempt to delete the dead metadata.json contract outright was dropped because the supporting evidence was flawed: a claim of zero writes across twenty-six runs counted twenty runs that predated the field’s existence. This fix instead rests on two facts that don’t depend on that count — there is no reader for the file, and three of its six fields already live elsewhere.

What’s new

Section titled “What’s new”

Features

Section titled “Features”

The review pipeline now validates its own run-level artifact instead of trusting it by convention. ce:review writes two kinds of artifact — per-persona records, which the parent has always validated before persisting, and the run-level review-summary.json, which nothing checked. An audit of 26 runs found 138 per-persona files sharing 21 shapes (111 identical), against 7 run-level artifacts with 7 distinct shapes written under two different filenames.

The run artifact now has a Zod source of truth, with the input ledger modeled as a discriminated union on record_type so admitted rows and rejected-payload summaries are machine-separable without inferring state from which keys happen to be present. A generated JSON Schema is committed and gated against drift, and validation ships as a new CLI command, systematic validate-review-artifact <path>, distinguishing four outcomes — valid, schema violation, operational failure (missing file, malformed JSON), and pre-contract legacy artifacts with no schema_version. Error output is projected through an explicit allowlist so validation failures never echo review content back into logs. The ce:review skill now requires the parent to stamp schema_version and run the validator immediately after writing, with a stated failure path: repair and re-run, never report a verdict over a failing artifact, and never delete it to dodge the check (#830).

Documentation

Section titled “Documentation”

Project docs had drifted from the tree they describe: skills were listed as 45 against 31 on disk, agents as 51 against 37, unit tests as 20 against 59 (later corrected again to 56 to match this branch), and integration tests as 2 against 11. Two script roles were also swapped in a way that could mislead a reader following them — build-registry.ts was documented as the drift checker, when drift is actually checked by generate-registry.ts (which regenerates registry.jsonc from skill and agent frontmatter), while build-registry.ts builds the OCX packument from the already-synced file. Undocumented parts of the tree — the Pi extension entry point, the evals harness and runner, and the codegen/drift-check scripts for Pi personas, the agent-browser skill, and the review artifact schema — are now described, and a script that only exists on an unmerged branch was removed from the list. Every backticked repository path in both files was checked for existence against this branch rather than spot-checked (#831).

Renovate’s package rules now give release-pipeline packages a minimum release age of three days before they’re picked up, and group semantic-release and conventional-changelog-conventionalcommits major updates under a single rule so they land together rather than piecemeal. A follow-up fix adjusted the package matching to include semantic-release-export-data for more accurate dependency management (#835).

What’s new

Section titled “What’s new”

Bug Fixes

Section titled “Bug Fixes”

ce:review’s Stage 5 verdict could read as clean even when a review had actually degraded, for three separate reasons closed by this release (#818).

First, environment-value redaction was too aggressive: it matched any runtime environment value, exact or embedded, and discarded an entire persona payload on a hit. Short values are common — in a typical shell, 19 of 101 environment values are eight characters or fewer, including strings like 0, 1, 3, 30, and -c — so a finding that merely quoted a diff line containing a digit could cause a reviewer’s whole payload to be thrown away. Value matching is now limited to values of at least 16 characters that are not purely digits, dots, dashes, or path separators, plus any value whose variable name looks secret-bearing regardless of length. Structural detectors are unchanged, and a match inside a single finding now drops only that finding rather than the entire payload.

Second, a rejected reviewer could still contribute to a “clean” verdict. When the persona assigned to a risk-critical surface came back malformed or never returned, the coverage note recorded the gap but the verdict itself did not reflect it. The verdict is now blocking unless another persona covered the same surface with validated evidence, and the same rule applies when a risk-critical persona loses findings to finding-level rejection. A follow-up fix refined this rule further: keying the block on any nonzero rejected-finding count was both too strict (blocking the verdict over a single dropped P3) and too loose. The rule now keys on severity — a rejected P0, P1, or unknown-severity finding blocks the verdict, while P2/P3 losses are only recorded in Coverage, and unknown severity fails closed.

Third, rejected payloads no longer get per-finding ledger entries, so deduplication — which runs only over validated returns — can no longer undercount cross-reviewer agreement by excluding an enumerated rejected finding from the fingerprint group of an identical surviving one. A rejected payload now rolls up into a single weighted summary entry, keeping disposition counts consistent with the findings actually observed.

The secret-bearing variable-name list used for redaction also gained coverage for common short-secret variables — DB_PASS, MYSQL_PWD, GPG_PASSPHRASE, SIGNING_PASSPHRASE, AUTH_SALT, and HMAC_SALT — via new _PASS, _PWD, PASSPHRASE, and _SALT patterns, underscore-qualified specifically to avoid catching benign names like BYPASS_CACHE, PWD, BASALT_DIR, or SALT_ROUNDS.

What’s new

Section titled “What’s new”

Bug Fixes

Section titled “Bug Fixes”

Agent and command discovery walked every .md file it found, so a plain README.md dropped into agents/<category>/ became a dispatchable agent named README and shipped as a registry component (#816). README is documentation by universal convention and was never meant to be content. Four independent code paths had reimplemented the same “every .md is an agent” rule — runtime agent discovery, command discovery, the overlay inventory that validates user config, and the content-integrity predicate that decides which files must satisfy the agent frontmatter contract — and each had to be corrected. They now share one helper. The integrity gate still scans README files for reference-integrity and banned-pattern checks; only the agent frontmatter contract is relaxed, so a real agent missing temperature: still fails the gate. The issue surfaced while adding a README to agents/review/ to record that the directory is a shared persona pool rather than a review roster.

The same change consolidated the synthesis artifact contract to one canonical home at skills/ce-review/references/synthesis-artifact-contract.md. It previously lived in three places that could drift apart; SKILL.md and review-output-template.md now summarize and link instead of restating the rules, and findings-schema.json remains the executable definition. AGENTS.md also now documents the generated-surface cascade — editing an agent description or body drifts the registry and the Pi persona fixtures, and adding a file under a skill’s references/ drifts the registry’s per-component file list — each of which was previously discoverable only by hitting a red gate.

Continuous Integration

Section titled “Continuous Integration”

A content-integrity check now fails the build when prose tells an orchestrator to pass a model argument to the dispatch tool (#815). The dispatch tool accepts a fixed set of arguments, and model is not among them — prose instructing an orchestrator to pass one degrades the dispatch to a generic sub-agent with no configured model, which silently discards the user’s per-agent and per-category model assignments. Three instances of this had already shipped; one survived a fix, a ten-persona review, and an automated review pass, and was found only by reading the published package rather than the source tree. The new check requires two co-occurring signals on the same line — a model: <value> assignment written as inline code, and vocabulary indicating a sub-agent dispatch — since either signal alone is ordinary in legitimate content. The vocabulary list deliberately omits the bare word “agent” (used constantly in legitimate docs about “bundled agents”), and model: inherit is exempted as a frontmatter literal that skills must name precisely in order to prohibit it. Requiring the assignment to sit inside an inline-code span, rather than merely following a colon, separates a real code-shaped argument from ordinary prose that would otherwise trip a false positive on a gate with no advisory channel.

The docs build and deploy jobs stopped reinstalling system packages the runner already has (#814). The docs job spent sixty seconds preparing a browser to render two Mermaid diagrams and only ten seconds building the site itself — almost all of that cost came from Playwright’s --with-deps flag, which runs apt-get update and installs CJK, Thai, and Cyrillic fonts plus a fontconfig trigger pass for diagrams whose labels are English. The flag is dropped; if a required library ever does go missing, Chromium now fails at launch instead of degrading quietly, keeping the failure visible. The remaining cost — the browser binary download — is now cached against the lockfile that pins Playwright, so a cache hit skips it and only a version bump triggers a fresh download. The same treatment was applied to the docs deploy job.

Documentation

Section titled “Documentation”

Three release and verification learnings were captured in docs/solutions/ (#812). A release run had reported success while publishing nothing: the job conclusion was green, and the release tool’s own closing line named a version and channel that did not exist in the registry, because that line prints in dry-run mode too — two workflow defects produced it, each hiding the other, so the behavior split by branch while ignoring the caller’s input in both directions. Separately, verification delegated into a fresh worktree had reported a malformed dependency import and three dozen failing tests that turned out to be an empty node_modules, not real breakage — a brief that names a fresh environment now has to name its preparation too, and has to let the reply distinguish a gate that failed from a gate that could not run. And publishing a fix for an older major was documented as resting on one fact: dist-tags play no part in semver range resolution, so a consumer on a caret range receives the newest matching version whether or not a tag points at it, which allows a one-shot release under a throwaway tag that is then deleted, leaving the default install untouched. The existing document on measured counts also gained a second instance — a test suite reading the developer’s own config file showed the configuration factor escaping version control, not just the filesystem factor it previously named alone.

Bug Fixes

Section titled “Bug Fixes”

The ce:plan reference documentation still instructed orchestrators to dispatch research agents with a model argument on the Agent tool — an argument that doesn’t exist in the tool’s schema. When present, the dispatch silently degraded to a generic sub-agent with no configured model, which then inherited the session model and discarded the user’s per-agent and per-category model assignments (#813).

This is the same defect previously reported in #784 and fixed across two skills in v3.10.2. That earlier pass missed this occurrence because it lives in a reference file rather than a skill body, and it was only caught this time by inspecting the published package rather than the source tree — the same line had already been corrected on the v2 maintenance branch by a wider sweep. A full sweep of bundled skills and agents confirms no remaining instance. The content-integrity gate checks that bundled agents omit a model field in frontmatter and validates literal subagent_type values, but nothing yet inspects prose for instructions to pass an unsupported argument — worth closing in a future pass.

Continuous Integration

Section titled “Continuous Integration”

The release job’s dry-run flag ignored the value passed to it, in both directions: a dispatch from the default branch always published regardless of what the caller asked for, and a dispatch from any other branch never did (#810).

Two causes masked each other. The workflow expression relied on operator precedence that doesn’t hold — && binds tighter than ||, and a workflow_dispatch input arrives as a string, so inputs.dry-run && 'true' evaluated truthy even when the caller passed false. The flag was therefore always true; the expression now compares against the string explicitly and parenthesizes the intent. A later step then forced the flag back to false whenever the run was on the default branch, which is what made real releases work at all and is why the first bug stayed invisible — but it also meant an explicitly requested dry run on the default branch performed a real release. With the expression corrected, that override step is redundant for every event the workflow handles, so it was removed rather than left to contradict the input. Pushes to the default branch are unaffected: they carry no inputs and evaluated false both before and after.

Bug Fixes

Section titled “Bug Fixes”

Every agent reference is now dispatchable on the v2 line. This is a backport of the v3 fix for the dispatch failures reported in #784, for users who can’t yet move to v3 because it removed bundled skills and agents they still depend on.

Three defects were fixed, each of which caused a dispatch to silently do the wrong thing instead of failing loudly:

  • Twenty-four agent references carried a ce- prefix that never matched any agent file, so every one of them failed to resolve. They’re now written in the qualified form the integrity gate actually validates, so they resolve and can’t rot again unnoticed.

That parameter doesn’t exist in the tool’s schema, so the dispatch silently fell back to a generic sub-agent with no configured model, which then inherited the session model — discarding per-agent and per-category model assignments without any error. Model policy is user-owned configuration, so the skills no longer try to set it.

This release adds no ongoing v2 support line: the release configuration change is scoped to this branch, publishes under a throwaway dist-tag that’s removed afterward, and leaves the default install pointing at the current major.

What’s new

Section titled “What’s new”

Bug Fixes

Section titled “Bug Fixes”

ce-plan: closed two escape hatches in the prior-art survey contract (#809). Both had shipped as known limitations, and neither needed new machinery to close.

The first hatch was in the exemption for plans with no survey section. That exemption exists because every plan written before the contract lacks the section, and without it none of them could execute — so the exemption is load-bearing. But it applied to any plan lacking a section, so a plan authored afterward with the section simply deleted got the same free pass, preserving exactly the duplicate-work outcome the survey exists to prevent. Since every plan already records its own date, the exemption is now conditional on it: a plan dated before the contract keeps the pass, one dated after must carry a survey, and a plan whose date cannot be established stops rather than guessing in either direction. The five states a plan can be in are now enumerated as an explicit partition, each mapped to exactly one branch, replacing prose that review had found self-contradictory.

The second hatch was in the survey itself. Because the agent chooses its own search boundary, one that preferred building something new could select a narrow but defensible scope excluding an existing equivalent, find only weak candidates inside it, and legitimately conclude nothing sufficient existed — every step defensible, the verdict worthless, and invisible because the survey recorded only what it searched, never what it declined to search. A verdict of building new now requires recording the adjacent scopes that were deliberately not searched, each with a reason; an empty list explicitly means no adjacent scope exists. Plan review now asks whether the concern would plausibly live in one of the excluded scopes, turning a private choice into a reviewable claim.

The survey contract’s version was bumped alongside the shape change, since making a field conditionally required changes what the contract describes, and leaving the version unchanged would have taught future readers that the field doesn’t track shape.

Documentation

Section titled “Documentation”

solutions: recorded three verification lessons from the prior-art survey work (#808), plus broadened one existing document to match what the round showed.

An exemption must be predicated on the condition that actually makes verification impossible, not on a signal that usually accompanies it. A gate comparing documented plugin hooks against registered ones had exempted any assertion saying “all” or “every” as a proxy for “asserts completeness without enumerating” — but a document claiming all six hooks while listing three matched the proxy, was fully checkable, and passed clean anyway. The predicate now names the real condition: the section enumerates nothing comparable.

A stop condition comparing current state against earlier state requires the contract to record that earlier state. A rule refusing stale survey results had shipped against a schema with no timestamp, revision, or digest, so the check could only ever report that freshness was unknown. The fix specifies the recorded baseline, how current state is computed, and what happens when comparison is impossible, in the same change as the rule.

Design review and literal-text review find different defect classes. Nine specialist reviewers assessed the ce-plan change above and found real defects; an automated reviewer then found that the shipped paragraph contradicted itself, scoping validation to plans that have a section and then treating an absent section as a halt. The design was right and the reviewers were reviewing the design — when prose is the enforcement mechanism, reading the final wording as an executable contract is a separate pass.

The generated-artifact drift document previously covered description edits only. Editing an agent or skill body drifts the Pi export fixtures too, because the export embeds full persona text, and adding a file under a skill’s references directory drifts the registry, which records per-component file lists — both invisible to targeted tests by construction. The generator source behind the drift claim was also cited directly.

What’s new

Section titled “What’s new”

Features

Section titled “Features”

This release grounds ce:plan in existing code before it lets a plan proceed, closing a gap where an agent could plan a duplicate of a subsystem it never looked for. Planning now dispatches a prior-art scope alongside its existing research: the survey receives the concern as trigger, effect, state, and boundary rather than a proposed design, so it cannot inherit the planner’s framing and can’t quietly confirm a solution shape it was handed. It bounds itself to a workspace and a stated budget, collects every plausible candidate before dispositioning any of them, and describes what each one owns in the vocabulary the code itself uses — because a subsystem named in accounting terms is invisible to a search framed in enforcement terms, even when its files are in view.

The survey’s result is a validated JSON contract, not prose: a missing or malformed block now gets a specific remediation instead of dissolving into unverifiable narrative. Five verdicts are available and the schema constrains what each may claim — building something new requires naming the candidates that were insufficient, an unpickable scope requires naming the scopes that were weighed, and running out of budget preserves whatever was already found rather than discarding it. A unscoped or unresolved verdict now stops planning until the scope narrows or a user explicitly accepts the uncertainty, and that acceptance is recorded so later stages can tell it apart from a verdict nobody handled. The survey also carries a freshness record — a version-control reference or a portable baseline — so work execution can refuse a plan whose surveyed scope has drifted since the survey ran, and plan review confirms each named candidate resolves to real code rather than taking the survey at its word. Plans written before this contract still run; a missing survey section is treated as pre-dating it, not as a failure.

Alongside the survey, the content-integrity gate gained two new checks against root documentation. One compares the hooks a document claims the plugin registers against the typed inventory the plugin entry point actually returns — closing a hole where a document could assert “all hooks” while enumerating only half of them and still pass. The other compares the modules named in the architecture codemap against the modules on disk in both directions, so an undocumented module and a stale codemap entry for a deleted one both fail the build. Together these catch the exact failure mode that motivated them: four contributor-facing documents claiming the plugin registers three hooks when it registers six, with the three unmentioned hooks being the ones the workflow guard runs on.

Documentation

Section titled “Documentation”

The documentation gap the new content-integrity checks were built to catch is fixed in the same window: ARCHITECTURE.md, STRUCTURE.md, .github/copilot-instructions.md, and AGENTS.md all previously claimed the plugin registers three hooks, when src/index.ts registers six — including the three observation hooks (tool.execute.before, tool.execute.after, and event) that the workflow guard depends on. An agent orienting from any of those documents could reasonably conclude the plugin has no enforcement path. ARCHITECTURE.md now describes the workflow guard directly: what the observation hooks feed, how operations get classified, what a receipt proves, and that it’s OpenCode-only. The project-local documentation-generation skill had also hardcoded “three hooks” into its own template, which meant regenerating ARCHITECTURE.md would have restored the error; the template now derives hooks from src/index.ts at generation time instead of carrying a frozen list.

A separate solutions entry records three verification boundaries discovered while shipping the dispatch-identifier gate. First, the release pipeline has two stages with opposite commit-body ingestion: release-notes-generator reads subject lines only, but the release-notes-narrative skill (the one producing this note) reads every commit body and, when thin, the originating PR description — so a commit body does reach the published notes, just through the second stage rather than the first. Second, releaseRules is scope-aware while presetConfig.types is not, so a non-releasing commit can still earn a notes section; v3.11.0’s Documentation section opened by quoting an internal planning label for exactly this reason. Third, tsconfig.json scopes typecheck to src/**/* only, leaving the eight files under scripts/ — including content-integrity itself — untypechecked; a deliberately injected type error and a call to an undefined function both passed bun run typecheck silently.

What’s new

Section titled “What’s new”

Features

Section titled “Features”

The content-integrity gate’s checkReferenceIntegrity validates references shaped systematic:<category>:<name> against real agent files, but anything spelled differently was invisible to it — 24 phantom ce--prefixed references and a subagent_type: Explore pointing at nothing sat in bundled content while the gate reported clean. v3.10.2 fixed those instances by hand, but the mechanism that let them rot in the first place was unchanged.

This release adds checkDispatchIdentifiers, closing the two decidable parts of that gap: a literal subagent_type value must resolve to a bundled agent filename stem, and an inline-code kebab-case token that ends with a real bundled stem but isn’t itself resolvable is flagged as a near miss. Both checks are deliberately narrow — deciding whether arbitrary prose refers to an agent is undecidable, and structural exclusions (path tokens, canonical references, skill directory names) keep the gate quiet without an allowlist to maintain.

The gate’s safety no longer rests on the coincidence that no bundled agent is named plan or review. Skill directories like ce-plan are now excluded explicitly rather than relying on an unenforced naming invariant that would have broken every ce-plan reference the moment an agent named plan shipped.

The change also fixes skills/using-systematic/references/opencode-profile.md, which had demonstrated dispatch using explorer and fixer — agents this package doesn’t ship. Readers without those agents in their own OpenCode configuration would follow the example and hit an unresolvable dispatch; the examples now use bundled agents so every reader can run them.

Review surfaced four defects that fixtures missed, all reproduced before fixing: quoted property keys never matched (so {"subagent_type": "x"} passed unchecked), the unquoted-value branch didn’t stop at a quote, updateFenceMarker kept only the first fence character, and a single path token suppressed near-miss detection for every token sharing its inline-code span. Verified against the real pre-fix tree: restoring the two files that shipped with 24 violations reproduces exit code 1.

Documentation

Section titled “Documentation”

Plan item I5 is marked complete. Every approach bullet has shipped: src/lib/source-model-defaults.ts and src/lib/model-availability.ts were deleted rather than narrowed, no provider-name routing survives in src/ (v3.10.0), every bundled agent reference resolves under checkReferenceIntegrity, and the model: task-tool parameter that silently bypassed user model policy is gone (v3.10.2).

Two sets of provider literals remain deliberately: JSON Schema examples in config-schema.ts documenting the provider/model shape for users writing config, and sample application code in skills/agent-native-architecture/references/ that teaches tiered agent design. Removing either would make the artifact worse, not less market-pinned.

The dispatch-identifier gap (see Features, above) was folded into this plan item because unresolvable references bypass model policy, making bad routing the visible symptom. With every instance closed, the residual is scoped down to the reference-integrity gate itself and filed as a standalone issue rather than left as an open-ended initiative.

A follow-up fix made the verification snippet in that second doc portable by replacing BSD-only sed -i '' syntax with perl -pi -e, which behaves identically on GNU and BSD systems, and added the restore-and-recheck step that had been described but not shown.

What’s new

Section titled “What’s new”

Bug Fixes

Section titled “Bug Fixes”

ce:review artifact contract enforcement (#798). Across 24 recorded review runs, only 11 of 19 qualifying runs produced any synthesis artifact and just 5 recorded which reviewers contributed to a merged finding; one run logged 22 findings and 8 named outcomes with no disposition for the other 14. Of 252 findings in the corpus, 60 had blank why_it_matters, 58 had empty evidence, and 3 artifacts were Markdown wearing a .json extension. The root cause: sub-agents wrote artifacts directly and nothing validated what landed. On Pi this never worked at all — every review persona declares tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash, which resolves to no write capability, while sub-agents were instructed to write a file anyway.

Persistence now lives in the parent orchestrator. Sub-agents return a single inline payload; the parent validates it against a tightened JSON Schema and writes it. A follow-up review found the original schema’s enforcement claim was empirically false — a payload with a 50,000-character field, an absolute path in evidence[], a 10,000-entry array, and injected unknown fields still validated as valid: true. The schema is now fully closed: additionalProperties: false on every object, maxLength/maxItems derived from observed corpus maxima, and path rejection covering absolute POSIX, drive-letter, and UNC forms. The contract is also split into a subAgentReturn shape (forbids forged provenance fields) and a parentRecord shape (requires them).

Three persona descriptions were also corrected: architecture-strategist, pattern-recognition-specialist, and code-simplicity-reviewer live under agents/review/ but are never selected by ce:review — their real consumers are ce-compound, deepen-plan, and ce-plan’s deepening workflow. Tests grew from 11 to 35 across the series, pinning each schema constraint at both the rejecting and accepting boundary rather than only asserting valid === false.

Documentation

Section titled “Documentation”

Captured verification blind spots from the model-defaults wedge — three failure modes that passed every automated gate at the moment they mattered. A new eval case registered at all documented touch points still let an integration test fail because it kept a hand-maintained verbatim copy of runner help text with nothing linking it to the source. A regression gate built to catch reintroduced source-owned defaults checked the model field but not variant, so a variant-only regression would have passed clean. And a dependency field annotated “retained for compatibility” had no reader anywhere, while a commit’s hardening rationale was silently erased by the next commit deleting that file — both examples of prose making claims no type, test, or linter evaluates.

Published 2026-08-17 · Updated 2026-08-17 · View on GitHub

What’s new

Section titled “What’s new”

Bundled agents stop being pinned to a Systematic-chosen model — they inherit whatever model invoked them, closing out a six-unit removal plan alongside a documentation drop on two release-pipeline traps discovered while shipping it.

Features

Section titled “Features”

Systematic no longer picks a provider/model pair for bundled agents on the user’s behalf. SOURCE_CATEGORY_MODEL_DEFAULTS used to map five agent categories to ordered provider chains, resolved against discovered availability before user overlays applied — and when nothing matched, it fell back to returning the first provider’s first model anyway, so a user on a provider Systematic didn’t enumerate could get pinned to a model chosen for someone else (an anthropic-only user invoking a design agent landed on vercel/v0-1.5-md). That table encoded the August 2026 model market as package policy, in tension with a harness whose thesis is “get better as models get better.”

The table, its schema, resolver, docs formatter, and the src/lib/model-availability.ts availability subsystem it depended on are all deleted. The config hook now performs no network call and no model-cache filesystem read, and agent resolution begins at category overlays with no source layer beneath them — category and exact-agent overlays, precedence between them, model: null restoring inheritance, and permission reconstruction all behave identically to before. This is a removal for plain npm consumers specifically: OCX/OMO installers keep curated category routing through their registry profile, while plain npm users lose category-aware routing unless they opt in. docs/src/content/docs/guides/model-defaults-migration.mdx records all five former provider chains (with variants) so any prior pin can be reproduced in explicit config.

A new model-inheritance eval case gates the behavior against regression, grading all 37 bundled agents across all 5 categories rather than a sample, and checking both model and variant together after an initial version of the gate proved less than its commit message claimed — it observed model but not variant, so a regression reintroducing variant pinning without a model would have passed clean. Agent identifiers from the eval manifest are now validated fail-closed against the live bundled inventory before being persisted.

Documentation

Section titled “Documentation”

Two traps surfaced while shipping the bootstrap catalog deletion, both quiet enough to reach main unnoticed, are now captured as solution docs. The first: this repository’s PR title decides whether a change publishes at all — squash merges are the only merge mode, squash_merge_commit_title is COMMIT_OR_PR_TITLE, and @semantic-release/commit-analyzer reads that header. refactor looks like a releasing type in presetConfig.types but isn’t one; a user-visible payload reduction nearly merged under refactor: and would have published nothing. The second: evidence collected against a pinned external runtime expires when the pin moves. The host-pin drift guard fired when main bumped OpenCode to 1.18.18, and the correct response was to move the pins and re-run the real-host eval suite rather than bump constants to silence the guard.

The existing gh heredoc doc now also covers git commit -m, since the backtick trap that mangles commit bodies (and the release notes they carry) is a shell rule, not a gh-specific one. The bootstrap catalog deletion and local eval foundation plans are marked complete.

What’s new

A performance-focused release: Systematic trims a redundant chunk out of every bootstrap prompt now that OpenCode’s native skill discovery covers the same ground.

Performance Improvements

Section titled “Performance Improvements”

Systematic no longer injects an <available_skills> block into the bootstrap prompt. OpenCode already registers bundled skills under native skills.paths, renders its own permission-aware catalog, and the systematic_skill tool description exposes the same names and descriptions — so the bootstrap-injected catalog was pure duplication. Removing it cuts the generated bootstrap payload from 18,145 to 6,232 characters and eliminates 23 absolute machine paths from prompt output.

renderCatalogVerbose() and formatSkillsXml() are removed along with their supporting escaping helpers, and CatalogEntry no longer carries path and skillFile, since those fields only existed for the deleted verbose path. The receipt-workflow fixture now requires exactly one opening and one closing workflow marker and verifies retained systematic_skill discovery guidance in place of the removed bootstrap catalog. ARCHITECTURE.md documents the per-harness discovery semantics this change relies on: OpenCode and Pi discovery surfaces, the unavailable-tool contract, and host-upgrade revalidation requirements — Pi has no registerSkillsPaths() equivalent, so denying systematic_skill removes the remaining catalog discovery path there.

The eval host pin moved from 1.18.5 to 1.18.18 to match the repository’s @opencode-ai/plugin and @opencode-ai/sdk dependency versions, and a drift check now fails the build if the pin and dependency version diverge. Because host catalog rendering is version-dependent, the bootstrap-catalog deletion was re-proven rather than assumed: the real-host eval suite passes 51/51 at 1.18.18, with the host still covering every bundled skill.

Published 2026-08-15 · Updated 2026-08-15 · View on GitHub

What’s new

Section titled “What’s new”

Features

Section titled “Features”

The evals harness now records bounded prompt-composition evidence and models three distinct observation states for each catalog check — present, absent, and impossible — instead of collapsing the latter two together. Previously, a run where the coverage signal simply couldn’t be observed was treated the same as a run that observed no coverage at all, which masked infrastructure problems as real coverage gaps.

Systematic and OpenCode catalog evidence is now partitioned by workflow-block containment, and that partitioning fails closed on malformed or unmatched blocks. This guarantees that Systematic-rendered catalog content can never be miscounted as host-runtime coverage, even when a workflow-block marker is broken or missing.

A new permanent host-skill-coverage case performs host-catalog coverage on the pinned runtime as exact set inclusion against the raw bundled skill names. Extra host entries are tolerated, but missing entries fail the case and are explicitly named in the failure output, and the case manifest is drift-protected by deriving expected names from the live bundled catalog at test time — so the manifest can’t silently go stale as skills are added or renamed.

Execution failures are also now split into two categories: diagnosed task failures (including host runtime timeouts) and undiagnosed infrastructure failures when no transform is observable at all, giving clearer signal about where a failing eval run actually broke.

This release also lands a fast differential test that feeds a shared corpus — including valid markers, unmatched markers, nested markers, duplicated Systematic catalogs outside the workflow block, mixed host/Systematic catalogs, and non-string entries — through both the typed TypeScript catalog-observation logic and the generated JS that actually executes in the spawned host, to keep the two implementations from drifting apart. A positive control ensures the test can’t pass by having both implementations return the same “impossible” state. The probe artifact identifiers (probeId and probeDigest) were also bumped to v3 so persisted run artifacts map cleanly to the implementation revision that produced them.

This work covers eval observation and gating only; no production behavior under src/ changed in this release.

What’s new

Section titled “What’s new”

Features

Section titled “Features”

Added a local OpenCode outcome runner for evals (#778), giving the project a deterministic way to execute and verify evaluation cases against local OpenCode runs without any telemetry or upload. The runner covers two cases — bootstrap-loading and fixture-local-write — each executable in both source and installed (packed-installed) modes, with distinct provenance tracked per mode so results are traceable back to how the code under test was actually running.

Fixture isolation is scoped rather than OS-sandboxed: child-process environment inheritance is denied by default, with explicit allowlisting required for test execution. Fail-closed behavior is enforced throughout — archive and dependency-resolution handling, privacy redaction, residue/quarantine cleanup, and manifest persistence all default to blocking rather than silently succeeding on the unsafe path. Signal-safe lifecycle handling was also wired in to guarantee best-effort cleanup of fixtures, spawned processes, and installed artifacts if a run is interrupted mid-flight, and outputs are written only to local run artifacts under evals/runs/<runId>/.

Follow-up review findings were folded into the same change: eval child-environment inspection was made CodeQL-safe by passing dynamic fixture values through argv instead of the environment, OpenCode secret matching was narrowed from a broad sk-* token regex to explicit sk- / sk_ shapes to cut false positives, and a regression test was added confirming legitimate skill-loading remains allowed while token-shaped sk values are still rejected.

What’s new

Section titled “What’s new”

Systematic gains a read-only diagnostics surface — a way to ask the CLI “what do you actually see?” without touching bootstrap, config resolution, or the plugin’s write paths.

Features

Section titled “Features”

systematic capabilities — deterministic, privacy-safe CLI diagnostics. The new cli-capabilities.v1 command exposes a versioned JSON snapshot of package/config/discovery state that was previously only inferable by reading source or guessing from behavior. It reports which skills and agents “won” discovery, separates config source presence from proven per-field authority, and surfaces bounded discovery failures — all without exposing discarded entries, local file paths, or other information that would leak privacy-sensitive details.

The diagnostic is strictly observational: bootstrap, config handling, setup, routing, and workflow protection behavior are all unchanged. Config loading was extended with read-only observation metadata, injectable roots, and warning sinks, and discovery keeps its existing winner semantics — failing closed on agent collisions and modeling malformed skill sources as bounded issue facts rather than crashing or silently dropping them.

This work also lands three new planning documents under docs/plans/ (the “Bitter Lesson” migration program, the capability-diagnostic plan itself, and a focused local OpenCode eval-foundation child plan) that capture the dependency-ordered modernization initiatives this feature is part of, along with the safety and evidence gates required before any related cleanup work proceeds.

Along the way, a CLI fixture-tree test was hardened: Bun 1.3.14 writes its own module-resolution cache under $HOME/.bun as a side effect of spawning bun src/cli.ts as a subprocess, which was tripping a byte-identical fixture-tree snapshot assertion. The .bun cache directory is now excluded from the snapshot — it’s Bun’s own runtime artifact, not something the CLI under test writes, so ignoring it doesn’t weaken the actual security assertion that the CLI writes no unexpected files.

Bug Fixes

Section titled “Bug Fixes”

The workflow guard’s marker parser (parseMarkerBody) hard-rejected any persisted marker whose protocolVersion didn’t exactly match the current MARKER_PROTOCOL_VERSION (2), with no fallback for v1 markers minted before PR #741’s version bump.

A user resuming an OpenCode session across the upgrade would carry v1 markers into v2 code, where the read path treated them as malformed, aggregating to guard-unavailable and dropping an in-flight guarded unit instead of recovering it.

Since MarkerSource’s shape didn’t change between v1 and v2 (the version bump was coordinated with an unrelated receipt-envelope schema bump), a persisted v1 marker recovers identically under v2 parsing. This fix mirrors the existing LEGACY_RECEIPT_PROTOCOL_VERSION pattern already used in receipt-ledger.ts: parseMarkerBody now accepts both MARKER_PROTOCOL_VERSION and a new LEGACY_MARKER_PROTOCOL_VERSION, with test coverage added for a persisted v1 marker parsed under v2 code.

A single security-scoped patch drives this release: a High-severity denial-of-service advisory in the js-yaml parser is patched, alongside routine automated dependency maintenance.

Bug Fixes

Section titled “Bug Fixes”

  • security: js-yaml is bumped from the resolved 4.3.0 to 4.3.1, patching GHSA-5p4m-2wfm-xmqj (CVE-2026-59870, CVSS 7.5, High). The advisory is in resolveYamlOmap(), whose key-uniqueness check does a linear scan per element when resolving YAML !!omap sequences — making the operation O(n²) overall. Because !!omap is part of the default YAML schema, any yaml.load() call is exposed without special options; a roughly 2.5MB crafted document can block the Node.js event loop for around 10 seconds. js-yaml is used directly in src/lib/frontmatter.ts to parse skill, agent, and command frontmatter, so this was real attack surface for anyone feeding untrusted skill/agent files through Systematic.

    4.3.1 back-ports the same Set-based key-tracking fix already shipped in the 5.x line (since 5.2.1) and satisfies the existing ^4.1.1 semver range in package.json, so the fix is a lockfile-scoped patch bump with no source changes required. It is independent of the pending major-version migration tracked in #733 (js-yaml v5), which additionally requires an import-shape fix for a dropped default export and is left to the normal Renovate/category-1 repair path.

    Verified on the fix branch: typecheck, lint, bun test tests/unit (1827 pass), build, content-integrity, and an ESM default-export smoke test all passed.

Features

automation: Fro Bot’s scheduled repository stewardship and autohealing have been consolidated into a single daily agent pass (#748). Previously the bot ran a separate Monday maintenance schedule alongside its daily autoheal run; that split schedule, dispatch mode, and prompt are gone, and stale-item detection, workflow-health checks, and repository metrics now all feed into one daily autoheal report. The consolidated pass combines proactive detection with bounded reactive repair (schedule-only issue healing, deduplicated, capped at a one-PR mutation budget per run) and adds progressive-improvement tracking that compares each report against prior reports, solutions, and recurring failures over time. Cross-project intelligence was also expanded, surfacing evidence-backed adopt/monitor/reject dispositions rather than raw signal, and agent-targeted follow-ups were replaced with cold-start notes any LLM agent can pick up without prior context.

To keep this safe to run unattended, the change enforces exactly one canonical Daily Autohealing Report (migrating any bot-authored legacy weekly/daily reports), constrains automatic issue triage to read-only analysis, and prevents checkout credentials from persisting across steps. Two follow-up commits harden this further: report-continuity tests were added to guard the new report lifecycle, and autoheal report writes were made atomic so a crash or interrupted run can no longer leave a corrupted or partial report file on disk. Scheduled and manual agent runs are now serialized so they cannot overlap, and GITHUB_TOKEN permissions remain read-only, with writes continuing to flow through the dedicated FRO_BOT_PAT.

What’s new

Section titled “What’s new”

Bug Fixes

Section titled “Bug Fixes”

Guard: canonicalize apply_patch paths in operation fingerprint (#747) — An apply_patch operation could fail closed to guard-unavailable, minting no implementation receipt, when a co-installed plugin’s before-hook rewrote the patch file path (absolute↔relative) before the receipt guard observed it. The guard fingerprints apply_patch arguments over the raw patchText string, so the before-hook fingerprint (computed over the rewritten output.args) and the after-hook fingerprint (computed over the original input.args) diverged, causing takePendingOperation to seal the operation as abandoned.

The fix canonicalizes apply_patch path targets to their lexical absolute form (via path.resolve against the effective session location, not realpath) before fingerprinting, at both prepareOperation and finishOperation. The patch body, target ordering, move destinations, and all non-path arguments remain part of the hash, so a changed patch body or a different target file still changes the fingerprint. Ambiguous or unparseable patches fail closed, leaving args unchanged.

Four regression tests cover the relative-before/absolute-after mint-once case, a changed body producing unavailable, a different file producing unavailable, and an equivalent duplicate after-event replaying without a double mint — exercising the before/after args divergence that the existing unit and integration suites (which feed fixed args directly to the guard) never covered. A follow-up commit adds two more regression tests closing gaps flagged in review: hunks-array form canonicalization including move_path, and fail-closed behavior for a malformed patch with an empty file-target path.

Bug Fixes

Section titled “Bug Fixes”

Fixed a bug where apply_patch operations targeting an absolute path inside a registered nested worktree would fail closed to guard-unavailable when no workdir argument was given. The root cause: deriveApplyPatchTarget seeded the shared-root set with the parent checkout root, so even though per-file targets correctly resolved to the worktree, a mismatch between the parent and worktree paths made sharedTargetRoot return undefined.

The fix derives the shared root from the patch-file targets alone when workdir is absent and the patch names files, matching deriveFileOperationTarget’s existing handling of write/edit operations. Behavior is otherwise unchanged: an explicit workdir, or a patch with no file targets, still seeds the workdir root, preserving both the multi-worktree spanning guard and the parent fallback for fileless patches. (#744, closes #743)

Published 2026-08-03 · Updated 2026-08-03 · View on GitHub

What’s new

Section titled “What’s new”

Bug Fixes

Section titled “Bug Fixes”

The receipt guard now correctly attributes worktree-targeted operations to the worktree they actually touched, closing out issue #678 end-to-end. Previously, child operations that acted on a registered worktree could have their receipts rolled up under the parent observer’s identity, and ambient GIT_DIR/GIT_WORK_TREE environment variables could spoof which repository an observer subprocess believed it was operating in. The fix introduces validateRegisteredWorktree (checking common-dir identity, git worktree list membership, and .git linkage) and strips GIT_* variables from observer subprocesses before they run.

On top of that validation, deriveOpencodeOperationTarget resolves the actual worktree a bash/write/edit/apply_patch operation acted on — from workdir, filePath, path, or multi-file patch targets — and fails closed on escaping, mixed-worktree, or git-admin paths. rollupForegroundTask now snapshots each recovered child receipt’s authenticated operationTargetIdentity instead of assuming the fixed parent observer, and is fatal on workspace/target/registration mismatches while remaining skippable only for repository/worktree revision staleness after the target already matches.

Completion readback was the last gap: it now resolves a single effective completion observer — the pinned registered worktree for pinned units, the parent observer otherwise — and anchors both the global and remote final readbacks to that target’s revision, while workspaceIdentity stays the stable parent identity. This eliminates the cross-root false “worktree delta” that had been marking legitimate worktree-targeted evidence as stale, and adds defense-in-depth by requiring a pinned unit’s global readback to carry the pinned operationTargetIdentity.

Follow-up review fixes registered operation-target-mismatch in the REASON_CODES set so the reason round-trips at the host marker boundary instead of degrading to guard-unavailable, threaded operationTargetIdentity through the legacy single-readback parser, and replaced an unsafe cast with proper digest narrowing at the receipt envelope parse boundary.

Bug Fixes

Section titled “Bug Fixes”

The ce-review shared reviewer prompt previously encouraged open-ended surrounding-code investigation, which led reviewers to repeatedly re-read unchanged files and drift across a single unresolved area instead of converging on a verdict. This release enforces a bounded, diff-first prompt contract: investigators now treat the supplied diff as the primary source of truth, read each unresolved surrounding range only once, and re-read only when ambiguity remains or the file has actually changed.

The contract also requires a terminal conclusion path — reviewers must return a finding/verdict or an explicit blocker/residual-risk statement rather than broadening scope indefinitely. A contract test now pins these semantics in the content-integrity checks, and a live pressure review confirmed convergence after a single diff read (#737).

What’s new

Section titled “What’s new”

Bug Fixes

Section titled “Bug Fixes”

The operation observer used to discover a single Git directory and reuse it for both command execution and filesystem reads. In repositories with a separate Git directory (core.worktree), that conflation meant commands resolved paths relative to .git while file hashing used repository-subpath semantics — snapshots could go stale or be reported unavailable, breaking readback and closure checks. This release (#735) splits command execution context from filesystem context: commands now use the discovered Git command directory, while file reads use the resolved worktree root. Tracked, staged, and untracked paths are now read with repository-root pathspec semantics (--full-name and :/) so snapshots stay repo-wide even when the command directory points at a subdirectory, submodule revision reads use absolute paths to avoid resolution drift, and remote readback operations share the same Git invocation root as local snapshot collection.

Continuous Integration

Section titled “Continuous Integration”

Renovate PR builds previously ran a separate artifact-generation step outside the normal build pipeline. That path is now consolidated into the standard build so Renovate PRs produce artifacts the same way any other PR does, and a postupgrade script/task was added now that bfra-me/renovate-action 10.1.0 supports allowed post-upgrade commands (#725). The Renovate and update-repo-settings workflows were also bumped to v4.16.44 (#734).

Bug Fixes

Section titled “Bug Fixes”

Protected workflows could fail closed after a successful foreground task delegation. Child receipts were being compared against the parent session’s salt and boot-time revisions, so stale intermediate receipts aborted the entire rollup, and explicit operation requirements declared after skill activation weren’t preserved across recovery. This release validates foreign child lineage and reconstructs receipt identities with the child session salt, preflights receipt batches before minting so stale mutable revisions are skipped while foreign workspaces stay fail-closed, and re-attests current child evidence against the parent’s live pre-task state without exposing a classifier bypass to model tools. Explicit starts can now monotonically extend pristine auto-started units — including resource scopes — with replay-safe recovery, and exactly-once rollup behavior is preserved across duplicate callbacks and host restarts. Test coverage was hardened to use semantic integration checks in place of model-wording-sensitive and raw marker-count assertions (#719).

What’s new

Section titled “What’s new”

Bug Fixes

Section titled “Bug Fixes”

Fixed a workflow-guard recovery bug that surfaced when Systematic was registered twice in the same OpenCode session — for example, when the published package (via user config) and the repo source (via project config) were both loaded. Both registrations had been appending receipt markers into the same shared, unnamespaced metadata array, so on restart each registration saw the other’s seed during recovery, misread it as a conflicting-seed, and forced the runtime to unavailable. The guard reported guard-unavailable even when protected config was active, and both registrations failed closed.

Recovery now classifies markers collected from session parts into own, provably-foreign, or ambiguous, and each registration recovers only its own markers, filtered by registration digest, instead of treating a foreign registration’s markers as a conflict. This is applied on both the main-session recovery path and the foreground-task child rollup path. Ambiguity still fails closed: if no own seed is resolvable and any marker is malformed or seedless, recovery still reports guard-unavailable rather than silently resetting the guard and risking state loss or corruption. Genuinely foreign-only marker arrays still start fresh, and the change is read-side only — the persisted marker format is unchanged and backward-compatible with existing sessions.
