Section titled “Documentation”

The public tagline was repositioned from “structured/compound-engineering workflows” to “Compound-engineering loops for OpenCode, Pi, and Claude Code,” applied uniformly across package.json, GitHub About (.github/settings.yml), the Claude Code marketplace and plugin/output-style descriptions, the README, the banner SVG, the docs site config and landing page, ARCHITECTURE.md, AGENTS.md, and the regenerated OCX registry. The pass also fixed stale harness lists that had named only OpenCode or only Claude Code, updating them to name all three shipped harnesses; runtime system-prompt prose was left unchanged.

Two new solution docs were added from the agent-browser vendoring work (v3.4.0): a best-practices doc on vendoring an npm-packaged upstream skill as a generated, drift-guarded artifact (pinned devDependency, copy from node_modules, CI drift gate, attribution version sync, Renovate postUpgradeTasks), and a test-failures doc covering an unguarded generator main() that silently repaired drift when imported by its own unit test, fixed with an import.meta.main guard. The generator entrypoint is now guarded with if (import.meta.main) so importing the script — as its own unit test does — no longer triggers generate-mode side effects that would silently rewrite skills/agent-browser/SKILL.md and ATTRIBUTIONS.md and mask real drift instead of detecting it.

Published 2026-07-27 · Updated 2026-07-27 · View on GitHub

What’s new

Section titled “What’s new”

Features

Section titled “Features”

Receipt-backed workflow completion guard (#697) — Workflow transitions (implementation, verification, commit, push, PR creation, check/review readback) are now grounded in host-observed evidence rather than self-reported state. A session-scoped, privacy-safe receipt ledger paired with an AST-bounded Bash classifier records real operations as they happen, and guarded transitions require runtime-trusted receipt minima before they’re allowed to complete. The guard fails closed on no-ops, replay, ambiguous shell shapes, and incompatible or stale receipt metadata — qualifying receipts are consumed exactly once.

Key pieces of the system:

  • OpenCode adapter wiring: a trust-bounded guard configuration supports observe/protected modes with project-scope protection, per-session/per-registration activation, and bounded workflow-control tools. Tool lifecycle hooks can surface blocks before execution while post-execution finalization never throws.
  • Operation evidence verification: current-state-bound before/after evidence, class-specific no-op and resource validation, and operation-aware staleness tracking ensure receipts reflect the true state of the workspace, repository, or resource in question.
  • Restart and recovery: receipts persist deterministically across restarts, with replay-safe readback, stale-evidence repair, and session-scoped projections. Foreground task child receipts roll up into fresh, parent-scoped, once-only evidence, failing closed on fork copies or mismatched lineage.
  • Local and remote operation observation: production write/edit/apply-patch and Bash verification/commit operations now mint real receipts using a stable-target/mutable-revision identity model and symlink-safe worktree hashing. Push, PR creation, and check/review readback observation use narrow, read-only git/gh JSON readbacks, storing digest-only resource identity and failing closed on unavailable or oversized readbacks.
  • Question attestation: a host-neutral, one-time attestation state machine (challenge → bind-asked → observe-reply → consume) gates certain transitions behind an exact-token yes/confirm reply, with replay and substitution protection and no retained user prose.
  • Skill-to-operation mapping: guarded skills are mapped to their required shipping operations on activation, with PR-check/review resource scopes deferred until the PR materializes and push upstream refs bound at start.

The guard also picks up several correctness fixes along the way: worktree digests now reflect working-tree content (not just the git index) so staleness checks stay accurate after staged edits; push classification recognizes more common git push command forms while still rejecting destructive refspecs (force/delete/mirror-like); and workflow observer subprocess calls now have bounded timeouts with fail-closed behavior. Configuration and generated documentation were updated to document the observe/protected/disabled modes, and CodeQL findings around predictable temp-file paths and a TOCTOU read window in test helpers were resolved using secure temp directories and readlink-first reads.

Both packages were pinned by markdownlint-cli’s own dependency ranges (js-yaml: ~4.1.1, markdown-it: ~14.1.1) and could not be resolved by bumping top-level version ranges alone — the fix required moving to markdownlint-cli@0.49.1, which requires js-yaml: ~5.2.1 and markdown-it: ~14.3.0.

The advisories addressed are quadratic-complexity denial-of-service issues: GHSA-52cp-r559-cp3m and GHSA-h67p-54hq-rp68 (high/moderate severity CPU exhaustion via YAML merge-key chains and repeated aliases in js-yaml), and GHSA-6v5v-wf23-fmfq (moderate severity DoS in markdown-it’s smartquotes rule). markdownlint-cli is a devDependency used for ad hoc Markdown linting and is not wired into the published plugin runtime or CI, so there is no production exposure. The change is scoped to a package.json version bump and a regenerated lockfile, with no source code changes.

Bug Fixes

Section titled “Bug Fixes”

The document-review skill now uses a single findings contract from reviewer output through synthesis. Previously, the shipped reviewer schema and prompts still produced legacy vocabulary — decimal confidence scores and auto/present autofix values — while synthesis expected the newer contract, so valid reviewer findings were misclassified as malformed and silently dropped.

This change makes the JSON Schema authoritative and aligns every producer and consumer surface to it: discrete confidence anchors (0, 25, 50, 75, 100), canonical autofix classes (safe_auto, gated_auto, manual), and consistent producer guidance, headless behavior, synthesis examples, and presentation templates across all seven reviewer personas. Legacy decimal confidence and auto/present values are now strictly rejected, and auto-class findings that omit a suggested fix are deterministically demoted rather than passed through inconsistently (#679).

What’s new

Bug Fixes

Section titled “Bug Fixes”

The build hardens Claude Code agent flattening: it now parses frontmatter and enforces uniqueness on the NFC + case-folded dispatch identity (both file stem and frontmatter name), failing closed when a name is missing, empty, or the wrong type. This guards against silent overwrites from case- or Unicode-folded collisions on case-insensitive filesystems. Bundle staging is now genuinely atomic — the prior bundle is renamed aside (not deleted) before the new one swaps in and restored on any swap failure — and the rename-aside step itself was folded inside the same try/catch so a stray staging directory can never leak, whether the failure happens in the write loop, the aside setup, or the swap itself. The SessionStart hook also drops its startup-only matcher so its declarative state facts fire on all sources (startup, resume, clear, compact), matching Claude Code’s own convention for the “all sources” form. No behavior change on the clean corpus (151 files, 37 agents, 31 skills). (#670)

Documentation

Section titled “Documentation”

This release ships an arc of workflow-first documentation across the banner, root docs, and docs site. The banner tagline now reads “Compound-Engineering Workflows for OpenCode, Pi, and Claude Code” (previously OpenCode-only), the empty Commands feature pill is replaced with Workflows, and the byte-identical duplicate banner in the docs site is removed in favor of a single source. (#668)

README, ARCHITECTURE, and STRUCTURE are brought current with the workflow-first framing across all three delivery surfaces. README now leads with the ce:* workflow as Systematic’s identity, with harnesses framed as supporting delivery surfaces; Quick Install gains the Claude Code marketplace path, and the First-Run Checklist is harness-agnostic. ARCHITECTURE documents the three-harness delivery model (OpenCode plugin, Pi setup, Claude Code CI-built marketplace bundle), and STRUCTURE adds the .claude-plugin/ directory and its build script. (#667)

The docs site landing page and Installation guide now lead with the ce:* compound-engineering pipeline (brainstorm, plan, work, review), demoting the supported harnesses to a supporting mention. The dedicated pi-harness and claude-code-harness guide pages are removed — their install steps folded into Installation, their boundary detail (Pi’s “honest parity differences”, Claude Code’s layered/capability-boundary model) consolidated into HARNESSES.md — with their URLs redirected to Installation. Usage sections across Installation are made harness-aware (prerequisites, asset discovery, first-workflow loop) rather than speaking only for OpenCode. (#666)

Two learnings from this docs arc are captured for reuse: authored .mdx GFM tables rendered as raw pipe text until remark-gfm was wired into the Astro markdown pipeline, and OpenCode’s plugin config key is singular plugin (not plugins) — the plural is silently ignored so the plugin never loads. (#669)

Bug Fixes

Section titled “Bug Fixes”

OpenCode’s config schema uses a singular plugin array, but the plural plugins key is silently ignored, so a configured plugin would simply never load. Several install docs and both shipped registry profile configs (standalone and omo) used the wrong plural key, which meant users following the documented setup ended up with instructions that failed silently. The docs and shipped configs — README, installation/index/agent-install pages, and the registry profile opencode.jsonc files — are now swept to the singular plugin key, aligning them with the behavior Systematic’s own setup.ts already enforces and its integration tests already exercise (#665).

Build System

Section titled “Build System”

Authored .mdx content pages weren’t picking up Astro’s default GFM table parsing, so pipe tables rendered as raw text inside a <p> element across the live docs site (configuration, main-loop, v3-migration, and others) instead of as actual <table> elements. Plain generated .md reference pages were unaffected. remark-gfm is now wired explicitly into markdown.remarkPlugins so .mdx content gets proper GFM table parsing — verified against built HTML output (configuration 0→1 tables, main-loop 0→1, v3-migration 0→2 tables), with no raw pipe-text tables remaining, mermaid diagrams unaffected, and all 85 pages building clean (#663).

Section titled “Documentation”

Two knowledge-track solution docs capture learnings from the Claude Code harness work: best-practices/claude-code-plugin-build-and-publish-architecture documents the build-and-publish-from-CI packaging pattern (gitignored staging, build-time identifier translation on generated output only, a generated-namespace integrity gate, release-gated orphan-branch publishing, SHA versioning, and the marketplace catalog), and workflow-issues/verify-installed-artifacts-not-just-build-gates captures the verification lesson that artifacts should be verified as-installed rather than assuming build gates passing is sufficient, and that unproven host channels should be probed empirically before designing against them. Both docs add reciprocal cross-links to the qualified-persona-ids, reference-integrity, and neutral-v1-gate sibling docs (#662).

Section titled “Continuous Integration”

The publish-claude-code-plugin job previously ran independent of the release job, so the plugin branch could ship a non-release commit, or drift from the published npm package if the release itself failed. The job is now gated on the release job and on an actually-cut version: semantic-release’s new-release-published/new-release-version are exposed as release job outputs, the publish job now depends on release, and publishing only happens when new-release-published is true. The plugin remains SHA-versioned — this change only couples its publish timing to npm releases (#661).

Features

Section titled “Features”

Systematic now ships as a distributable Claude Code plugin (#660). The work landed as a series of coordinated changes: a new Claude Code capability profile (skills/using-systematic/references/claude-code-profile.md) documents the harness’s verified mechanisms — name-based subagent dispatch, AskUserQuestion, the TaskCreate family, and native Skill/SKILL.md discovery — grounded in HARNESSES.md evidence and a live Desktop probe, resolving a previously-unverified subagent_type note. HARNESSES.md promotes Claude Code from Tier 2 to Tier 1 accordingly, with a new install guide covering the output-style/hook/native-skill channel model.

The bundle itself is generated, not committed: scripts/build-claude-code-plugin.ts mirrors the existing registry codegen pattern, walking skills/ and agents/ source to flatten 37 agents and copy 31 skills into a self-contained plugin, rendering an output-style from the using-systematic skill body plus the CC profile, and emitting a declarative SessionStart hook well under the platform’s size cap. After an initial approach that committed the bundle, the design was reworked mid-series into an ephemeral, build-time-translated artifact — identifiers are rewritten to Claude Code’s plugin-namespaced form (e.g., ce:brainstorm → systematic:ce-brainstorm), a generated-namespace integrity gate catches any untranslated reference, and the 151 previously-committed bundle files were removed in favor of gitignoring claude-code/ as build staging.

Distribution happens from CI: a .claude-plugin/marketplace.json on main points Claude Code at the built plugin on a dedicated claude-code-plugin branch, which a publish job fast-forwards on every push to main using the built-in GITHUB_TOKEN (no App token or PAT, and its pushes don’t recursively trigger workflows). Users install via claude plugin marketplace add marcusrbrown/systematic. Along the way, two dangling skill references (ce:debug, ce:polish-beta) with no bundled directory were found and neutralized, and a new content-integrity check now hard-fails the build if any ce:<name> reference fails to resolve to a real skills/ce-<name>/ directory — closing off that class of broken reference for good. Validation is covered by tests/integration/claude-code.test.ts, which checks shared-core fidelity, artifact self-containment, and that the build never writes to src/.

Section titled “Code Refactoring”

The ce-plan skill’s Phase 1.1/1.3/1.5 research-agent dispatch instructions used a fake function-call form (task systematic:research:X(...)) that read as literal, executable code on any harness (#656). It’s rewritten as prose (Dispatch \systematic::` — pass …) matching ce-plan's own existing dispatch-instruction style. The qualified persona IDs themselves are unchanged: they're the canonical, phantom-validated cross-reference form that checkReferenceIntegritychecks againstagents//.md`, and a broader bare-name conversion was investigated and reverted specifically because it would have dropped that validation coverage.

The other closes out the harness-portability plan from v3.1.0, adding the neutral-v1 marker and migrated-set identifier gate patterns, documenting a unit-suite-rewrites-repo-file trap that caused a double re-review on #653, and cross-linking related warning-channel and dry-run-integration docs (#655).

Features

Section titled “Features”

feat(skills): harness-portable skills — capability profiles, neutral spine, identifier gate (#653) implements the B′-thin portability increment (plan 2026-07-16-001):

  • Two capability profiles (OpenCode, Pi) live under using-systematic/references/, covering the four capabilities that diverge across harnesses: subagent delegation, blocking user interaction, task tracking, and skill loading. Both are inlined into the controlled bootstraps via BootstrapDeps.profileBlock inside the existing <SYSTEMATIC_WORKFLOWS> zone, snapshot-pinned and double-run idempotent.
  • using-systematic was migrated to neutral capability-resolution routing, dropping the two OpenCode-specific routing lines now that the bootstrap carries the harness binding.
  • orchestrating-subagents was structurally rewritten to neutral delegation language — all task( and subagent_type occurrences (12 and 8, respectively) were removed while preserving the substance of the skill.
  • The blocking-question idiom gained a Pi binding at 24 sites across 16 skills, and ce-review’s internally drifted site was normalized to match.
  • A new content-integrity check (#13) bans harness-specific identifiers in migrated-skill bodies (flagged via the harness-portability: neutral-v1 metadata marker). The check is fence-aware, exempts profile files inside fences, and exempts the sanctioned idiom parenthetical.
  • New Pi harness proof scenarios cover profile presence and cross-profile absence, migrated-skill activation payload scans, and sequential-delegation markers.
  • HARNESSES.md is a new evidence-backed harness registry: every tool name maps to in-repo lines, cloned/installed source, or an authoritative URL, with unverified capabilities explicitly marked. The profiles and AGENTS.md are cross-linked to it, and it now ships in the npm package alongside the profiles that reference it.
  • The skill registry was regenerated (73 components).

Follow-up commits in the same PR hardened the work against ce:review findings: isMigratedSkill now keys off the harness-portability marker only (closing a path where unrelated non-string metadata could disable check #13), the idiom exemption is identifier-aware so only blocking-question identifiers are exempt on sanctioned lines, a 9th banned pattern (backtick question) was added per the plan spec, and readHarnessProfile now emits a stderr diagnostic on read failure without ever throwing. A portable bootstrap-snapshot fix normalizes the resolved skills directory to a <SKILLS_DIR> placeholder so the pinned bootstrap bytes stay machine-independent, and a docs fix stops the unit suite from silently downgrading configuration.mdx’s $schema example from v3 to v2 on every local run — the generator test now runs against a temp copy and asserts the repo file is untouched.

Bug Fixes

Section titled “Bug Fixes”

The release-notes-narrative skill’s step-13 rollback gate previously asserted that a rewritten narrative body must be longer than the auto-generated body it replaced. That assumption broke on major releases: the v3.0.0 squash commit embedded its entire prose under BREAKING CHANGES in the auto-generated body (11,048 chars), so the correctly-rendered 4,394-char narrative was auto-rolled back by CI — the length gate rejected exactly the rewrite it was meant to protect (#644).

Step 13 now verifies the render contract structurally instead: the body must start with ## What's new, contain at least one recognized bucket heading, include the Compare link, and differ from the pre-edit snapshot. Length comparison is explicitly forbidden, with the v3.0.0 incident recorded as the rationale.

Section titled “v3.0.0”

Published 2026-07-17 · Updated 2026-07-17 · View on GitHub

What’s new

Section titled “What’s new”

Systematic 3.0.0 is the curation major: the bundled catalog is reshaped around the compound-engineering workflow core, the legacy conversion machinery is gone, and the same npm package now ships a second harness — the Pi coding agent.

Breaking Changes

Section titled “Breaking Changes”

The bundle is curated down to 31 skills and 37 agents (from 46 and 51). The Ruby/Every vertical (dspy-ruby, dhh-rails-style, andrew-kane-gem-writer, every-style-editor, ankane-readme-writer), peripheral integrations (rclone, gemini-imagegen, test-xcode, proof, feature-video, report-bug-ce, changelog, generate_command), stack-specific review personas (kieran-rails-reviewer, kieran-python-reviewer, dhh-rails-reviewer, julik-frontend-races-reviewer, schema-drift-detector, lint), duplicate standalone reviewers (security-sentinel, performance-oracle, data-integrity-guardian, data-migration-expert, cli-agent-readiness-reviewer), the Figma-dependent design agents, and the setup placeholder skill are removed. The todo trio (todo-create, todo-resolve, todo-triage) merges into a single todos skill, and writing-systematic-skills folds into writing-skills. (#611, #587)

Removed names fail soft. Referencing any removed skill or agent in disabled_skills/disabled_agents warns and is ignored instead of failing config validation, and the warning links the migration guide. Every removal is mapped to its replacement in the v3 migration guide. (#614)

The CC→OpenCode runtime converter and systematic convert CLI are removed (#612). Bundled content ships pre-normalized; the converter had been a no-op on every load since 2.32. The skill deprecation-warning machinery and the deprecated: frontmatter contract go with it.

Features

Section titled “Features”

Pi coding-agent harness support. The same @fro.bot/systematic package now loads in Pi via a pi manifest (extensions, skills): bundled skills surface as native Pi skills, systematic_skill resolves skill content through the shared resolver, the using-systematic bootstrap is injected into every session, and a new systematic_delegate tool runs bundled agent personas as in-process child sessions — fail-closed on unknown personas, capped at 20 turns, with least-privilege tool allowlists derived from each persona’s frontmatter. A setup --harness opencode|pi CLI command writes the project-local config for either harness atomically, with backup and idempotent re-runs. Where Pi parity honestly ends (no systematic.json config consumption, no permission gating in Pi 0.80.6) is documented in the Pi harness guide. (#623–#638)

The Pi integration is proven against the real runtime: an integration suite spawns the actual Pi CLI in RPC mode with a mocked model and asserts extension load, skill discovery, skill resolution, bootstrap injection, and persona delegation end-to-end from the packaged tarball. (#637)

Documentation

Section titled “Documentation”

The v3 migration guide maps every removed skill and agent to its replacement and covers the converter removal and config cleanup. The published JSON Schema moves to schemas/v3/ (the config $schema example now points at schemas/latest/).

What’s new

Section titled “What’s new”

A security fix for Pillow, plus a steady stream of tooling and dependency maintenance.

Bug Fixes

Section titled “Bug Fixes”

Pillow’s minimum version floor moves to 12.3.0, closing off resolution of versions vulnerable to five decompression-bomb / command-injection advisories (GHSA-8v84-f9pq-wr9x and related PIL PcfFontFile, FontFile, BdfFontFile, GdImageFile, and WindowsViewer issues; PYSEC-2026-2253 through 2257) that remained reachable under the previous >=12.2.0 constraint. 12.3.0 is the first Pillow release that patches all five advisories, and the bump directly addresses the OSSF Scorecard Vulnerabilities check flagged by code-scanning alert #28.

What’s new

Section titled “What’s new”

Bug Fixes

Section titled “Bug Fixes”

Discovered skills (a user’s or project’s own skills, registered as commands) were being labelled with the (Systematic - Skill) prefix, which falsely implied that Systematic had authored them. That prefix is now dropped entirely for discovered skills, and the command instead surfaces the skill’s own description as-is.

Bundled Systematic skills-as-commands also had their labelling tightened: the - Skill qualifier is removed, so their prefix now reads simply (Systematic), matching how bundled plain commands are already labelled. isSystematicCommandConfig was updated to recognize only the (Systematic) prefix going forward — the retired (Systematic - Skill) label needs no migration path, since OpenCode applies config-hook mutations in memory on each load and never persists them, so a previously-injected entry can never reappear in existing config. Discovered commands are consequently left unmarked and are added if absent rather than refreshed or cleaned across reloads, which is safe because every launch rebuilds the command config from disk and simply omits any skills that were deleted (#594).

v2.33.1

Section titled “v2.33.1”

Published 2026-07-07 · Updated 2026-07-07 · View on GitHub

What’s new

Section titled “What’s new”

A follow-up patch to discovered-skill command registration (#592): disabled_commands now actually suppresses discovered-skill commands, a single-read fix removes a redundant file read, and a CodeQL-flagged TOCTOU race in the same code path is closed.

Bug Fixes

Section titled “Bug Fixes”

Discovered skills register as slash commands under their bare name, but collectDiscoveredSkillsAsCommands was ignoring the disabled_commands field, so there was no way to suppress a single discovered skill’s command short of turning off the whole feature. The fix filters discovered-command emission by disabled_commands — the free-form field that governs command names — while leaving the stricter disabled_skills bundled-name enum untouched. The configuration guide now documents the split: disabled_skills governs bundled skills, disabled_commands governs discovered-skill commands.

The same follow-up also closed a file-system race CodeQL flagged (js/file-system-race) in the discovered-skill file read: a statSync check-then-readFileSync pattern left a time-of-check/time-of-use window. The pre-check is dropped in favor of reading the file directly — a directory throws EISDIR and a missing path throws ENOENT, both already handled by the existing catch, so the same skip behavior holds with one fewer syscall and no race window.

As a performance side effect, command-only discovered skills (e.g., skills with model invocation disabled) previously read their SKILL.md twice — once via extractFrontmatter during discovery, which discarded the body, and again via readFileSync in the inline command path. extractFrontmatterFromContent was split out of extractFrontmatter so the file is read once in toDiscoveredSkill, with the body carried on DiscoveredSkill for the inline command path to reuse.

Published 2026-07-07 · Updated 2026-07-07 · View on GitHub

What’s new

Section titled “What’s new”

Features

Section titled “Features”

Skills discovered from user and project locations can now surface as /slash commands, not just as model-invocable tools (#592, 142c090). A new discovery pass (src/lib/discovered-skills.ts) walks the same six roots OpenCode itself uses to find skills — global ~/.claude and ~/.agents, project .claude/.agents directories walked up to the worktree root, and .opencode config dirs — applying upstream’s own last-write-wins precedence (.opencode beats .claude/.agents beats global) so the command that wins matches what OpenCode’s skill tool would resolve. Discovered skills are gated behind a skills_as_commands toggle (on by default): model-invocable skills get a one-line shim that loads the skill via the native skill tool with $ARGUMENTS passed through as data, while command-only skills (those with model-invocation disabled) get the SKILL.md body inlined directly. Each generated command carries a (Systematic - Skill) ownership marker so re-runs stay idempotent and any user-defined command with the same name always wins. A follow-up review pass tightened the drop predicate for orphaned commands, honored user-invocable: false parity with bundled skills, bounded the discovery walk so it never climbs past the worktree root when there’s no git root, and filled in precedence and edge-case test coverage.

Continuous Integration

Section titled “Continuous Integration”

PRs targeting the long-lived v3 branch now get the full check suite and Fro Bot review: v3 was added to the pull_request.branches filter across the main, fro-bot, and CodeQL workflows (#584, 268e996). Push triggers stay scoped to main, so the release job still never runs against v3 — work in progress there can’t accidentally trigger a publish.

Documentation

Section titled “Documentation”

Plan housekeeping this cycle: a future-dated plan artifact (dated 2026-07-13, a week ahead of when it was written) was corrected to 2026-07-06, with its internal date, origin, and superseded_* cross-references fixed to match (#591, 75187a3). Separately, stale v3-adjacent plan statuses were reconciled: the removed-name config-safety plan had been left marked executed-pending-pr despite having shipped in #534 (v2.32.0), so it’s now marked completed with provenance, and an older v3-compatibility-cleanup plan was marked superseded by the newer v3-cleanup-release brainstorm, with superseded_at/superseded_reason frontmatter added for consistency with other superseded plans (#583, c02a0dfd).

Code Refactoring

Section titled “Code Refactoring”

The two worst noExcessiveCognitiveComplexity offenders in the codebase, validateFieldExamples (cognitive complexity 41) and extractFrontmatter (cognitive complexity 25), were split into file-local helper functions while preserving exact behavior, ordering, and exported signatures (#582, 77fbd7f). Repo-wide complexity warnings dropped from 6 to 4.

Bug Fixes

Section titled “Bug Fixes”

Biome 2.5.0 introduced two new error-level lint rules that would have blocked the pending @biomejs/biome dependency update (PR #538) from passing CI. This release pre-emptively fixes both violations before the dependency bump lands:

  • lint/a11y/noSvgWithoutTitle in docs/public/favicon.svg — Biome now requires SVG elements to carry an accessible title. Added <title id="favicon-title">Systematic</title> and the corresponding role="img" aria-labelledby="favicon-title" attributes so screen readers can identify the favicon.
  • lint/complexity/noImportantStyles in docs/src/styles/custom.css — Three !important declarations on .install-title (for margin, font-size, and color) were used to override Starlight’s heading specificity. Replaced with the higher-specificity selector .install-header .install-title, which beats the Starlight h3 rule without !important. Visual appearance is unchanged.

Merging this fix first unblocks the Biome upgrade PR from failing the Lint check.

Published 2026-06-15 · Updated 2026-06-15 · View on GitHub

What’s new

Section titled “What’s new”

Features

Section titled “Features”

Config validation now handles the full lifecycle of bundled skill and agent names — including names that have been removed in past releases. Previously, listing a no-longer-bundled name in disabled_skills or disabled_agents would fail validation and prevent plugin load, effectively bricking setups that had disabled something Systematic later cleaned up.

v2.32.0 introduces a removed-names mechanism with three coordinated layers:

  • Schema acceptance: The JSON Schema generator now includes the removed-names list in the enum for disabled_skills and disabled_agents, so editors and runtime stay in sync. While the list ships empty today, the schema will reflect any future additions without requiring editor configuration updates.
  • Validation acceptance: Removed names are accepted during config validation alongside current bundled names, maintaining the strict rejection of genuinely-unknown names.
  • Load-time cleanup: After validation, removed names are silently dropped from the effective disabled lists and a per-load [systematic] warning identifies each stale entry. Raw config is preserved for merge precedence; the dedup is stateless per load.

A content-integrity gate enforces that removed names never overlap current bundled names, preventing accidental misclassification as a name moves from active to removed.

What’s new

Section titled “What’s new”

Bug Fixes

Section titled “Bug Fixes”

The orchestrating-subagents skill has been updated to match the current behavior of OpenCode 1.17.6. A prior version of the skill documented a task_status polling tool that OpenCode has since removed. In OpenCode’s current model, background subagents (enabled via OPENCODE_EXPERIMENTAL_BACKGROUND_SUBAGENTS) push their results into the parent session automatically on completion — there is no status tool to poll. The skill’s background-dispatch guidance, failure/retry instructions, quick-reference section, and common-mistakes list have all been rewritten to describe this push-notification model accurately.

The same PR also adds an optional setup recommendation: enabling OPENCODE_EXPERIMENTAL_BACKGROUND_SUBAGENTS=true. The flag is experimental but stable in recent OpenCode versions, and without it Systematic falls back to foreground dispatch.

Documentation

Section titled “Documentation”

Plan documents were reconciled with shipped reality after v2.31.0: the agent temperature hardening plan now records its v2.29.0 provenance, the skill frontmatter tune-up plan is marked completed (shipped in v2.31.0), and the promotion-and-growth plan is marked completed with remaining ecosystem-listing work reframed as externally tracked upstream work.

Four test names in the JSONC-precedence suite carried AE1/AE2/AE3 prefixes that leaked internal planning taxonomy into the shipped test file. These prefixes have been stripped, leaving only the behavioral descriptions.

A solutions document was added capturing a durable lesson from the skill frontmatter tune-up work: scripts/content-integrity.ts has no general non-failing warning channel — every check other than allowlist warnings counts toward totalViolations() and fails CI. This makes “advisory warning” checks infeasible without building new plumbing. The doc records the end-to-end wiring checklist, the fence-aware body-scan pattern, and the meta-lesson: ground the mechanism a plan relies on, not just the intent.

Published 2026-06-07 · Updated 2026-06-07 · View on GitHub

What’s new

Section titled “What’s new”

Features

Section titled “Features”

The ce:compound-refresh skill now declares an argument-hint in its frontmatter, making its $ARGUMENTS interface visible to callers and the OpenCode command surface. This skill accepts a mode:autofix flag and an optional docs/solutions/ scope hint — both are now documented where they can actually be discovered. Beyond the hint itself, this change establishes which frontmatter fields are enforced: a new enforcement column in writing-systematic-skills/references/foundation-conventions.md clarifies that allowed-tools is parsed but not permission-gated, while argument-hint is now subject to content-integrity checking. A new guard fails any skill that references $ARGUMENTS outside fenced code blocks without declaring argument-hint, preventing the gap from recurring. The check correctly strips fenced code blocks first, so skills that merely document $ARGUMENTS in an example are not flagged.

Documentation

Section titled “Documentation”

A new solutions doc captures the reusable lessons from the npx skills install command rollout (v2.30.0–v2.30.1): how to make a load-side-effect generator testable by exporting the helper and guarding the entrypoint behind import.meta.main; driving the --skill selector from frontmatter name values; two MDX traps (a <name> placeholder in a table cell parses as JSX and breaks the table; copy buttons only attach to fenced code blocks, never inline code in table cells); and verifying rendered docs against built HTML rather than source or a blocking dev server. The doc cross-references the related MDX, codegen, and verification docs rather than duplicating them.

Continuous Integration

Section titled “Continuous Integration”

The release pipeline no longer fails when the release-notes narration dispatch confirmation times out. Previously, scripts/dispatch-release-notes.sh would exit 1 if it could not confirm the dispatched Fro Bot run within the poll budget — even though the dispatch had already succeeded and the narration had run. This happened on v2.30.1: the release published and the body was narrated correctly, but the job showed red because GitHub surfaced the dispatched run after the poll window closed. A successful gh workflow run call means the dispatch was accepted; failing to observe the run is an observability gap, not a dispatch failure. The confirmation timeout now emits a ::warning:: and exits 0. The poll budget was also bumped from 90s to 180s to reduce the race for future releases.

What’s new

Section titled “What’s new”

Features

Section titled “Features”

The docs site now surfaces npx skills as a first-class, portable install path alongside the OpenCode npm plugin. Previously, Systematic’s installation story pointed exclusively at @opencode/systematic, which is an OpenCode-specific runtime. Skills themselves are harness-agnostic Markdown content that work in any agent environment — OpenCode, Claude Code, Cursor, Copilot, or any other harness. The npx skills add marcusrbrown/systematic command installs that content directly from this repo, no registry required.

The homepage now presents a dual install-path block with chooser cues to help readers pick fast: “OpenCode, full runtime” for the npm plugin (still the recommended path for the complete OpenCode experience), and “Any harness, skills only” for npx skills. The Installation page gains a dedicated secondary section with a scannable flag table. The README Quick Install section reflects both paths. Every non-deprecated skill reference page now carries a copyable npx skills add marcusrbrown/systematic --skill <name> command, auto-injected by the docs generator — deprecated skills are correctly excluded and the generator change is covered by nine new unit tests.

Documentation

Section titled “Documentation”

A new best-practices solution doc captures the converter-injected default hardening pattern that emerged across v2.27.0 (agent mode) and v2.29.0 (agent temperature). Both cases followed the same shape: derive a runtime-injected default’s resolved value mechanically from the real inference function, write it explicitly into frontmatter, change the runtime to fill-if-absent, and add a content-integrity gate that requires the value to be usable — not merely present.

Two lessons are encoded for future reference. First, zero-behavior-change must be proven mechanically by deriving the expected value for every agent and asserting zero mismatches, not assumed. Second, a presence-only gate is a false lock: the runtime treats present-but-invalid values as absent and falls back anyway, so the gate must verify usability. The doc cross-references the two related overlay and gate best-practices docs.

What’s new

Section titled “What’s new”

Features

Section titled “Features”

Agent temperature is now explicit in every bundled agent’s frontmatter and respected by the runtime, removing a hidden inference heuristic that had been silently overwriting any hand-authored value.

All 51 bundled agents now declare an explicit temperature:. The 37 that previously relied on runtime inference have their resolved value written into frontmatter, derived mechanically from the same function the runtime used, so no agent’s effective temperature changes in practice. The config hook now reads that explicit value instead of always overwriting it, preserving the precedence chain: user overlay > explicit frontmatter > inferred fallback.

A content-integrity gate enforces the invariant going forward: every bundled agent must declare an explicit, finite-number temperature:, and the check fails closed on malformed frontmatter. This brings temperature to parity with mode, model, and color — each agent’s value is now auditable in source rather than computed invisibly at load time.

What’s new

Features

Section titled “Features”

The new orchestrating-subagents skill gives agents a portable, OpenCode-native primitive for coordinating both serial and parallel subagent work. It centres on task() dispatch as the default mechanism — foreground dispatch that works in any context — while documenting background subagents and task_status as experimental, gated surfaces for environments that support them.

Beyond the dispatch primitive itself, the skill covers the full coordination lifecycle: how to divide work across subagents without file overlap, how to track git ownership when multiple agents write concurrently, how to synthesise results from independent runs, and how to handle retry when a subagent stalls or fails.

The skill ships alongside a v3 compatibility cleanup plan that will remove converter-era compatibility surfaces and deprecated orchestration guidance now that the replacement is in place. Bundled skill surfaces, the OCX registry, and cloned OpenCode source metadata (pinned to v1.15.10) were all updated in the same change so the skill is discoverable immediately. (#491)

Section titled “Features”

mode: subagent is now declared explicitly on all 51 bundled agents. Previously, 36 agents relied on the OpenCode runtime converter to fill in mode: subagent as a default at load time — an invisible dependency that would silently break when the converter is removed in v3.0.0. Without an explicit mode, those agents would fall back to OpenCode’s native default (all) and appear as primary agents in the agent picker rather than staying hidden as background workers.

This is a zero-runtime-behavior-change hardening. The converter already resolves these agents to subagent, so making the field explicit changes nothing today while severing the converter dependency for the future. To lock in the invariant, a new checkAgentMode gate in scripts/content-integrity.ts fails CI if any bundled agent is missing an explicit mode: subagent, sets a non-subagent value, or has non-object frontmatter. A converter-equivalence test mechanically proves the change is behavior-preserving by resolving agent config both with and without an explicit mode and asserting the outputs are identical.

The PR also records a tracked audit of every other field the converter injects — notably temperature, which is computed per-agent via a name/description heuristic and represents an equally high-risk dependency for v3.0.0. Resolving the temperature dependency is out of scope for this patch; the audit exists so it is not forgotten.

Documentation

Section titled “Documentation”

A new solution doc under docs/solutions/ captures the undecidability lesson from the content-integrity verification work: some YAML frontmatter problems cannot be detected by parse-diff analysis alone.

The concrete case: a truncating comment (problem: cache miss # under load, where the author intended the full string including # under load) and a legitimate inline comment (date: 2026-01-01 # created) are byte-identical to the YAML parser — both parse to the text before the #. No amount of parse-diff analysis can distinguish “lost content” from “intentional comment.” Rather than ship a heuristic that would silently misclassify edge cases, the ban rule approach was taken: unquoted inline comments in solution-doc frontmatter are banned outright. This collapsed the detector to a simple lexical rule and removed approximately 50 lines of parse-diff guessing that could never have been correct.

The doc records the undecidability, the reasoning for the ban, and the general principle: when a detection problem is provably undecidable at the data level, a clear bright-line rule beats a heuristic that quietly gets edge cases wrong.

The bulk of this release is a promotion-and-growth push that turned the docs site into a real product landing surface. The homepage was redesigned around a custom hero, a live stats banner, and an aligned feature grid built on the existing OKLCH theme tokens — replacing the stock Starlight splash and fixing long-standing CSS issues where invalid :global() selectors in MDX style tags were silently dropped. A build-time stats emitter walks skills/, agents/, and the registry to publish live skill/agent/component counts and a git-tag-resolved version, so the homepage never renders stale or broken numbers. Quick Start was merged into a single canonical Installation page (with a redirect from the old URL), structured SEO metadata (Open Graph, Twitter cards, JSON-LD) was added, and a Privacy page now documents the cookie-free, self-hosted, DNT-respecting, no-PII analytics posture. The interior reference and guide pages were restyled to match the homepage’s restrained list-and-spacing language, and a stray OCX mention was removed from the homepage.

Several engineering learnings were captured alongside the docs work: an Astro Steps HMR regression and CSS-liveness verification guidance, a refreshed live-server QA learning emphasizing that an HTTP 200 is not a render signal, and updated static-preview guidance. The promotion-and-growth plan was reconciled against shipped provenance to track which units actually landed.

The two previously-separate Fro Bot workflows (fro-bot.yaml and fro-bot-autoheal.yaml) were consolidated into a single workflow handling all three operating modes — PR review, daily autohealing, and weekly maintenance — with inline prompt routing instead of a separate resolve-prompt job (#446). The release-notes-narrative automation contract is preserved verbatim: workflow_call still accepts the prompt and correlation-id inputs and resolves them at highest precedence. Follow-up changes documented two subtle invariants inline for future maintainers: why the workflow_call/workflow_dispatch prompt branches must precede the mode-gated branches (so external prompt-only callers like the release-notes automation aren’t silently captured), and why explicit fork-detection exists only for issue_comment events (the only PR-adjacent path where github.event.pull_request is null even when the issue is a PR).

Adds a docs:verify script that runs the exact three-command sequence the CI Docs Build job runs — bun install --frozen-lockfile, bun run --cwd docs playwright install --with-deps chromium, and bun run docs:build — so a docs-framework Renovate PR (Starlight, Astro, expressive-code, etc.) can be locally pre-verified before approval.

The motivation is concrete: PR #444 (Starlight 0.38→0.39) cleared every local gate — typecheck, lint, content-integrity, registry-drift, unit tests — and only failed at CI’s Docs Build step, because Starlight’s astro:config:setup hook runs exclusively under a real Astro build. The fix was straightforward, but the round-trip to CI cost time that docs:verify eliminates. This was the second such incident in two weeks.

The script is a single chained shell command rather than a separate shell file: zero new files, zero new dependencies, zero new documentation surface beyond the AGENTS.md line that names it. On a hot cache the whole run takes ~5 seconds; on a cold cache the Playwright Chromium download dominates (~30–60 s).

Bug Fixes

Section titled “Bug Fixes”

A CodeQL js/incomplete-multi-character-sanitization alert (#31) on docs/scripts/transform-content.ts had been stable in the weekly maintenance report for over five weeks. The cleanDescription helper was using a single-pass replace(/<[^>]+>/g, '') strip — the textbook shape the analyzer flags, because adversarial input like <<tag> survives one pass with the leading < intact.

The trust boundary here is real: this helper only runs against committed SKILL.md and agent frontmatter description fields, never against runtime user input. The fix iterates the strip to a fixed point so any residue from the first pass is caught on the next, and a comment above the loop documents the constraint explicitly for future contributors who might reach for the helper in a higher-trust context. No build output changed; docs:build still emits the same 110 pages.

What’s new

Section titled “What’s new”

Bug Fixes

Section titled “Bug Fixes”

The release-notes-narrative automation chain gains its fourth consecutive hotfix, this time replacing the log-scanning strategy for identifying dispatched Fro Bot runs with a timestamp-based approach.

v2.23.3 (#433) had resolved the HTTP 422 input-validation problem and Fro Bot’s dispatch was actually firing. But the polling loop in dispatch-release-notes.sh timed out after 90 seconds trying to match the dispatched run by scanning its early log lines for the correlation token. The token never appeared within that window because the Fro Bot OpenCode agent has a substantial bootstrap sequence — runner spin-up, full checkout, bun install, model/auth setup, and MCP server startup all happen before any prompt-derived content reaches the run’s logs.

The fix captures a DISPATCH_EPOCH timestamp immediately before gh workflow run, then polls gh run list --event=workflow_dispatch for the newest run whose createdAt is strictly greater than that epoch. Because gh run list reflects run-creation time rather than first-log time, the dispatched run is visible to the API as soon as it’s registered — long before the agent boots — so identification is reliable regardless of how long startup takes.

The correlation-id field is preserved as a secondary audit anchor. It’s still passed to gh workflow run and still declared in fro-bot.yaml, so it appears in the run’s inputs metadata for any future debugging session, but it is no longer the primary identification mechanism.

Test coverage was updated alongside the fix: makeRunListJson now accepts an optional createdAt argument and defaults to a far-future ISO timestamp so the default run is always selected by the timestamp filter; the scenario for correlation-via-log-scan was replaced with a “no run created after dispatch epoch” scenario (exit 1); and a new scenario was added for the newest-wins case when two runs have different future createdAt values. The suite grew from 19 to 20 passing tests.

A follow-up commit refreshed the block comment in dispatch-release-notes.sh (which still described the old log-scan strategy), updated the prompt body to drop the now-obsolete instruction to echo the correlation token, and renamed a stale test fixture suffix (scenario-18) to a scenario-agnostic name.

What’s new

Bug Fixes

Section titled “Bug Fixes”

The third hotfix in the release-notes-narrative v2 automation chain resolves the final blocker preventing fully automated post-release narrative generation.

After v2.23.2 published (which fixed the missing dispatch-release-notes.sh script), the Release CI job was still failing with HTTP 422: Unexpected inputs provided: ["correlation-id"]. The root cause: dispatch-release-notes.sh passes a UUID correlation token as a structured -f correlation-id=... workflow dispatch field so that the polling loop can identify the correct Fro Bot run, but fro-bot.yaml had never declared correlation-id as a known input. GitHub’s Actions runtime validates every field in a workflow_dispatch or workflow_call invocation against the workflow’s declared inputs: block and rejects any unrecognized name.

This fix adds correlation-id as an optional string input to both the workflow_dispatch and workflow_call entry points in fro-bot.yaml. The field is purely a polling correlation primitive — Fro Bot echoes it as its first log line so the dispatching script can scan early job output and match the run unambiguously, eliminating same-second collision risk. No existing entry point (PR comments, issue events, scheduled maintenance) is affected; they simply omit the field, which is valid for an optional input.

With this declaration in place, the end-to-end acceptance gate for v2 — where a published release automatically triggers Fro Bot to rewrite its notes — can proceed without operator intervention.

What’s new

Section titled “What’s new”

The release-notes-narrative v2 automation no longer crashes the Release job on bash parameter expansion. v2.23.0 and v2.23.1 both shipped to npm successfully but failed their Release job with SyntaxError: Unexpected token ':', because @semantic-release/exec renders the entire successCmd YAML block through lodash-es template() with no escape support — every ${...} in the bash script (including ${VAR:-default} parameter expansion and even ${...} inside comments) was being evaluated as a JavaScript expression.

The fix moves the dispatch logic out of the YAML scalar entirely. The successCmd: is now a one-line invocation of an external script:

scripts/dispatch-release-notes.sh receives the target tag as $1 and is otherwise a normal shell script — no Lodash collision surface. The only template interpolation Lodash sees is the one we want: the target version from semantic-release context.

This is the third hotfix in the v2 automation sequence. The two earlier attempts (#430 introduced the inline successCmd; #431 tried to fix it with backslash escapes) failed because Lodash’s default template settings have no backslash-escape semantics — \${VAR} still evaluates VAR as JavaScript and just leaves the backslash as a literal character in the output. Verified empirically by running template('\\${VAR}')({}) locally and observing the same is not defined error.

The 19 integration tests in tests/integration/release-notes-ci.test.ts continue to cover the full dispatch chain: tag validation, correlation-token generation, polling fallback, conclusion-taxonomy classification (success, neutral, failure, cancelled, timed_out, action_required, skipped), security signals (HTTP 401/403, off-target release edits, body-integrity check post-write), and unexpected gh run watch exit codes.

The fourth hotfix in this chain (still in flight at PR #433) addresses a separate production failure surfaced by this release: gh workflow run rejected the dispatch with HTTP 422: Unexpected inputs provided: ["correlation-id"] because the fro-bot.yaml workflow did not declare correlation-id as a valid workflow_call/workflow_dispatch input. That fix adds the input declaration. v2.23.2’s release notes you are reading right now were rewritten manually using the v1 skill procedure.

What’s new

Features

Section titled “Features”

A new project-scoped skill at .agents/skills/release-notes-narrative/ that turns sparse semantic-release output into useful changelog narrative. The skill is loaded on demand by any agent to patch a published GitHub release body via gh release edit --notes-file, defending against two known release-notes-generator failure modes already observed on this repo: bare bucket bullets (semantic-release ingests only commit subject lines, never commit bodies or PR descriptions) and spurious closes [URL-fragment] autolinks (the generator misparses path#fragment substrings in commit bodies as Closes #N footers).

The skill ships as a 13-step procedure with a hardcoded bucket map mirrored from .releaserc.yaml, a calibrated thin-commit-body threshold for triggering PR-body enrichment, and a 4-condition AST-based autolink-strip allowlist with documented positive and negative examples. Three-layer defense for the live gh release edit step (pre-edit snapshot, preflight check, post-edit rollback) keeps blast radius bounded. Structural idempotence — same buckets, same Compare link, same referenced PRs across reruns — is the explicit guarantee; LLM-generated narrative prose is allowed to vary by run (#429).

This release is itself the first dogfood: the skill was applied to v2.20.5, v2.20.6, and v2.21.0 retroactively as acceptance evidence before merge, and the v2.22.0 release notes you’re reading now are the skill’s output.

2.19.0 (2026-05-18)

Section titled “2.19.0 (2026-05-18)”

Deprecations

Section titled “Deprecations”

Two bundled skills are now marked deprecated with removal: v3.0.0 (target not committed to a specific timeline). Both remain functional in v2.19.x — invoking either now emits a one-time console.warn per OpenCode session naming the planned removal and (where applicable) the replacement.

  • orchestrating-swarms → replacement: orchestrating-subagents (will land in the v3.0.0 cycle). Documents CEP’s Teammate API primitives (TeammateTool, spawnTeam, TaskCreate/TaskList/TaskGet, team_name parameter on task(), Claude Code subagent_type names) that do not exist in OpenCode.
  • claude-permissions-optimizer → no replacement planned. Targets Claude Code’s ~/.claude/settings.json allowlist mechanism. OpenCode uses a SQLite-backed session-scoped permission model with built-in always-persistence; there is no prompt-fatigue analog and no OpenCode equivalent to optimize.

Migration: When v3.0.0 ships, the rescue path is standard semver: install @fro.bot/systematic@^2.19 while migrating. v2.18.x and v2.19.x remain on npm.

If v3.0.0 never ships, the deprecation warning becomes the new steady state and both skills stay bundled.

New: skill deprecated: frontmatter field

Section titled “New: skill deprecated: frontmatter field”

Optional deprecated: block on SKILL.md with shape { since, removal, replacement?, reason? }. Runtime parser is permissive (silent drops on malformed values, never throws). Content-integrity gate is strict for bundled skills: since, removal, and reason must all be non-empty strings — mirrors the runtime drop rules so any bundled skill that passes the gate also produces a runtime warning.

Warning format when systematic_skill loads a deprecated skill:

Replacement: and Reason: clauses appear only when set. Dedup via a closure-scoped Set<string> so each deprecated skill warns at most once per OpenCode session.

1.0.0 (2026-01-26)

Section titled “1.0.0 (2026-01-26)”

⚠ BREAKING CHANGES

Section titled “⚠ BREAKING CHANGES”
  • Command names and agent paths have changed

Content Changes:

  • Pull CEP skills: agent-browser, agent-native-architecture (with references/), brainstorming, compound-docs (with assets/references/), create-agent-skills (with references/templates/workflows/), file-todos, git-worktree
  • Remove skills: writing-plans, test-driven-development, systematic-debugging, verification-before-completion, executing-plans, using-git-worktrees, writing-skills
  • Pull CEP commands: workflows/{brainstorm,compound,plan,review,work}, agent-native-audit, create-agent-skill, deepen-plan, lfg
  • Remove sys-* prefix from commands - now /workflows:plan instead of /sys:plan
  • Restructure agents into review/ and research/ subdirectories

Code Changes:

  • Add CLI convert command for converting CEP content to OpenCode format
  • Update findAgentsInDir and findCommandsInDir to support nested directories
  • Commands in subdirs use category:name format (e.g., /workflows:plan)

Documentation:

  • Update README with new content tables and conversion instructions
  • Update using-systematic skill with available content reference
